Audyt wykazał, że oba składniki wskaźnika wymaganego przez H-E nie były dostępne jednocześnie w żadnej z pięciu fal programu HFCS. Depozyt ma charakter dokumentacyjny: nastąpił po zamknięciu rozpoznania i nie pełni funkcji preregistracyjnej. Udostępnia procedurę, bez której wynik negatywny pozostawałby nieweryfikowalny — czytelnik nie mógłby sprawdzić, czy zbiorów szukano właściwie. Na tej samej procedurze opierają się dwa opracowania wykazane w aneksie preregistracyjnym monografii: inwentarz par zmiennych o pojemności różnicowej oraz procedura datowania statusu zmiennych w kolejnych falach badania. ——— English summary. Protocol for task 0.4 of the research programme accompanying the monograph „Situational awareness in the housing market“ (in Polish), with two annexes, the outcome of the dataset review and an audit of HFCS variable catalogues. The task was designed as a partial, surrogate test of two core hypotheses on existing household panel data. The review closed with a null result for Poland: none of the datasets examined measures the household planning horizon, nor does any contain an objective measure of financial competence. The audit shows that the two components of the differential indicator required by hypothesis H-E were never simultaneously available in any of the five HFCS waves. This deposit is documentary, not a pre-registration: it was made after the review had closed and makes no claim of priority. It publishes the procedure, without which the null result could not be verified.

Virtual environments are often added to exercise equipment to make exercise more engaging, although previous work has often emphasised enjoyment. This exploratory within-subject study compared stationary cycling with screen-based virtual cycling in 15 adults (6 women, 9 men; aged 20–59 years). Each participant completed one 10-min, self-paced session in each condition, in counterbalanced order, on the same recumbent bicycle with fixed resistance. After each session, participants completed the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory and rated their perceived exertion (Borg 6–20); heart rate and cadence were recorded every minute. Enjoyment was higher after virtual cycling (mean difference 2.31 points on a 1–7 scale, 95% CI [1.61, 3.00]), as was value/usefulness (1.38 [0.56, 2.20]); 14 and 12 participants, respectively, reported higher scores. Both paired t-test differences remained after Holm correction. Differences in perceived competence, effort/importance, and pressure/tension were smaller, with confidence intervals including zero. Heart rate (4.9 bpm, 95% CI [-0.04, 9.8]) and cadence (2.8 rpm [-2.4, 7.9]) showed no clear difference between conditions. Perceived exertion was slightly higher during virtual cycling (0.8 points [0.01, 1.59]), but this difference did not remain after correction. Power output was not measured, so workload could not be compared directly. Enjoyment was strongly correlated with value/usefulness during virtual cycling (r = 0.87, 95% CI [0.64, 0.95]); individual responses also varied, particularly in perceived competence. Given the small sample and single 10-min session per condition, larger studies should measure workload directly and examine responses across repeated sessions.

Background Systematic review software must coordinate independent human decisions, protocol amendments and heterogeneous information sources. Synchronizing reviewers at every stage can create waiting time unrelated to the scientific assessment of a record. We describe R-SYS, a workflow that links decisions to versioned protocols and allows reviewers to progress independently before a final reconciliation step. Methods The reference implementation combines an eleven-phase guarded lifecycle, immutable locked protocol versions, deterministic rendering of a canonical search strategy, per-reviewer working sets and decision provenance. Each primary reviewer advances through title and abstract screening, full-text assessment, extraction and risk-of-bias appraisal using their own preceding decisions, subject to human adjudication. A final convergence checkpoint resolves outstanding work before synthesis. Artificial intelligence (AI) supplies advisory recommendations that are excluded from human reconciliation. We analyse completion times under explicit scheduling assumptions and describe implementation limitations. Results With identical task sets, continuous reviewer availability and no external waiting, independent lanes achieve a completion time equal to the largest reviewer workload. This is a lower bound for schedules that impose additional synchronization constraints. Disagreement can introduce superseded work and delays; a sufficient condition for retaining an advantage over stage barriers is stated. The implementation provides mechanisms for protocol change control, reviewer coordination and traceable reporting. No empirical measurements of accuracy, efficiency, usability or cost are reported. Conclusions R-SYS provides a reference design for separating reviewer independence from workflow synchronization. Its theoretical scheduling properties do not establish practical time savings, search completeness or AI accuracy. A separate, prospectively specified validation study is planned after completed reviews using the platform become available.

Diagnostic radiologists spend much of their professional time interpreting imaging studies using a variety of workstation and monitor configurations. Despite well-established ergonomic principles, there are no widely accepted recommendations regarding monitor configuration, application placement, or peripheral device selection. This variability, particularly across academic medical centers with diverse workstation configurations, may contribute to musculoskeletal injury, workflow inefficiency, cognitive burden, and challenges integrating artificial intelligence (AI) applications. This study characterizes radiologist workstation configurations and determines whether similar usage patterns emerge across two independent national needs assessments. The findings from both assessments were compared. The first consisted of live audience polling during an RSNA 2025 educational session on radiologist ergonomics ( n = 54). The second was an online survey distributed through professional LinkedIn and radiology social media communities ( n = 49). Survey questions evaluated monitor number and orientation, workstation layout, application placement, ergonomic practices, sit–stand workstation use, and peripheral devices. Both assessments demonstrated similar workstation preferences. Most respondents in both the RSNA poll ( n = 54) and online needs assessment ( n = 49) used four-monitor equivalent configurations consisting of two portrait diagnostic monitors (often combined into one 30″ landscape) flanked by two supplemental monitors. Dictation was most commonly displayed on the left supplemental monitor, adjacent to the current examination (on the left diagnostic monitor). Respondents reported diverse placement of worklists, thumbnails, AI tools, peer review, electronic medical records, and advanced visualization applications. Sit–stand workstations were widely used, with most respondents standing 10–30% of the workday. Gaming mice with hyperscrolling functionality were the predominant pointing devices with very similar functions (window/level, measure, arrow, zoom/pan, and ROI). Two independent national needs assessments revealed consistent patterns in radiologist workstation configurations despite differences in survey methodology and participant populations. These findings suggest an emerging, flexible de facto standard that could guide ergonomic recommendations, workstation design and procurement, residency training, workflow optimization, and AI integration.

documents.abstract: Persistent, channel-organized communication environments give instructors ways to arrange questions, assistance, announcements, and informal interaction alongside a learning management system. Their use depends on how students enter the environment, how information and audiences are organized, who provides assistance, and how participation is experienced. This conceptual article presents Real-Time Academic Platform Integration Design (RAPID), a descriptive framework developed through a focused synthesis of 37 publications and a source-anchored matrix of 750 evidence items. Following a bounded literature search with artificial intelligence support for screening and extraction, the authors reviewed source evidence and selected and refined the framework by comparing model-generated alternatives. RAPID comprises four components: Student Onboarding, Environment Organization, Sustainable Help, and Student Participation and Social Climate, interpreted through an affordance perspective and Community of Inquiry. A constructed LMS-centered baseline, two reflective teaching illustrations, and a literature-informed projection show how it applies across differences in course size, staffing, and participation requirements. The framework’s usefulness, workload implications, and relationship to learning require empirical study.

Introduction to Business is often a student’s first encounter with how organizations plan, take risks, communicate, and answer for their decisions. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how students research and write, and how colleges increasingly recognize neurodiverse ways of learning. Together these make the first business course a natural place to reconsider what introductory business education can be. This paper describes a redesign of BUS 101 at Barton College’s School of Business & Innovation, being delivered in Fall 2026 across three sections taught by three instructors. The redesign treats the course itself as a working business environment. Syllabus policies become exercises in applied risk ethics: a “24-Hour High-Risk Window” and a one-time “Stuff Happens Pass” modeled on a contingency reserve. Academic integrity rests on process rather than detection, through visible revision histories and a Socratic oral defense. Presentations carry 40% of the grade, personal finance is taught as a form of self-governance and a gateway to business finance, and qualitative video reflections complement numerical ratings. Shared cross-section sessions with industry speakers provide continuity while preserving each instructor’s approach. Drawing on process philosophy, the ethics of responsibility, and experiential learning theory, we set out the design’s rationale, its implementation to date, and a research agenda whose results will be reported in a follow-up study.

Large language models (LLMs) have clear potential to contribute to psychological research methods. However, as with any new research method, LLM-based methods require rigorous evaluation. Towards this end, Austin and colleagues evaluated the ability of two LLMs (GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash) to facilitate scale validation by identifying relevant criterion measures and generating validity hypotheses for assessing convergent and discriminant validity. We argue that their study has several key limitations that limit the conclusions that can be drawn about the proposed method's suitability for use in validation research. We situate our critique within three recommendations for incorporating LLMs into research: (a) avoid essentialisation and overgeneralisation about 'AI', (b) use application programming interfaces when evaluating LLMs in research contexts and (c) evaluate LLM-based methods using clearly specified criteria. Finally, we consider whether adopting the proposed method might reinforce or amplify existing limitations in the psychological literature, namely, the proliferation of overlapping constructs and inadequately validated measures.

Clinical AI is moving from systems that generate discrete predictions and recommendations toward agents capable of pursuing clinical objectives through repeated tool use, communication, planning, and state-changing actions. Emerging systems support multistep electronic health record workflows, and increasingly envision longitudinal care across repeated encounters. This transition expands safety assessment beyond discrete outputs and actions. Through its actions, an agent can help create the clinical state on which its subsequent decisions depend. Consequently, individually defensible actions may compose into an unsafe trajectory, even when no single action is clearly erroneous. We propose recoverability-centered trajectory governance as a clinical synthesis of established safety approaches, linking patient-specific corrective capacity to the continuing justification for delegated authority. Its central objective is clinical recoverability: preserving the opportunity for the human-AI care system to redirect care before clinically acceptable corrective pathways are exhausted. We define recovery margin as the remaining opportunity for such correction, and reauthorization boundaries as conditions requiring delegated authority to end or narrow pending renewed human judgment. This framing distinguishes reversibility, primarily a property of an action, from recoverability, a property of an evolving clinical trajectory. The operational framework combines persistent obligation tracking, independent monitoring, explicit reauthorization, authority contraction, graceful degradation, independent escalation, and verified human takeover. Oversight should concentrate at consequential trajectory junctions. Evaluation should combine trajectory stress testing, component-specific recovery-margin indicators, interruption-and-takeover testing, and population-level surveillance. Trajectory governance complements product lifecycle oversight by examining whether continued patient-specific delegation remains justified as care evolves. Because corrective capacity depends partly on access to timely monitoring and human rescue, recoverability is also an equity issue. The defining safety question is therefore not only whether an action is acceptable but whether continued delegation remains justified. The proposed indicators and governance mechanisms require domain-specific operationalization and empirical validation, including comparison with established safeguards.

documents.abstract: Australia’s growing demand for science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) skills contrasts with stagnant tertiary participation and persistent inequities. This brief review examines barriers to inclusive tertiary STEM education and the potential for artificial intelligence (AI) to support Universal Design for Learning. AI can provide multimodal content, personalised scaffolding, flexible participation and assessment, and support for self-regulated and collaborative learning. Effective adoption therefore requires institutional governance, AI proficiency and sustained educator judgement. Further longitudinal research in Australian tertiary STEM settings is needed to identify which tools reduce barriers, for whom and under what conditions.

Existing studies have primarily focused on the effects of artificial intelligence (AI) on productivity and carbon emission efficiency, while systematic evidence on whether and through which mechanisms AI improves agricultural ecological efficiency (AEE) remains relatively limited. Using provincial panel data from China for the period 2005 to 2023, this study employs the entropy weighting method to measure regional AI development and a slack-based measure (SBM) model incorporating undesirable outputs to evaluate AEE. A two-way fixed effects model is further constructed to examine the effects of AI on AEE and the underlying mechanisms. AI is conceptually distinct from general digitalization, automation, precision agriculture, and information technology development, as its defining feature lies in leveraging machine learning, intelligent sensing, and algorithmic decision-making to achieve more advanced data processing and intelligent decision-making capabilities. The results indicate that a 0.1-unit increase in regional AI development is associated with an average increase of 0.01078 units in AEE. Mechanism analysis suggests that AI can indirectly improve AEE by promoting green finance development and industrial structure upgrading. Furthermore, agricultural technological innovation exhibits a significant threshold effect, with higher levels of technological innovation strengthening the positive effect of AI on AEE. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that the positive effect of AI on AEE is more pronounced in eastern regions, regions with lower levels of urbanization and agricultural modernization, and non-major grain-producing regions. Further analysis identifies positive spatial spillover effects of AI on AEE in neighboring regions, contributing to coordinated green agricultural development across local and neighboring regions. This study provides evidence on the effects, transmission mechanisms, and threshold conditions through which AI improves AEE, offering new empirical insights into the role of AI in facilitating the green transformation of agriculture and extending the analytical perspective of agricultural sustainability research.

documents.abstract: This repository provides the complete Python implementation and verified experimental results associated with the research article entitled “AI-Based Bearing Fault Classification Using Vibration Sensor Data: Effects of Signal Representations and Decision Thresholds.” The study investigates the effects of dimensionless vibration features, signal representations, physical-time dynamics, and source-derived decision thresholds on artificial intelligence-based bearing fault classification. Experiments were conducted using 59 source recordings from the MCC5–THU three-phase asynchronous motor dataset and 32 target recordings from the University of Ottawa Electric Motor Dataset. Five predefined feature and temporal configurations, 11 classification models, and four decision rules were evaluated. The models include physical-time spiking neural networks, a memoryless SNN counterpart, conventional machine learning classifiers, and ensemble methods. Model training, calibration, and decision threshold selection were performed exclusively on source data using nested stratified group cross-validation with three outer folds and two inner folds. The trained models were evaluated on the Ottawa recordings without target-side parameter updates. The Ottawa analyses include exploratory comparisons at the recording level. The archive contains: The complete Python source code and software dependencies. Publication Figures 5–10 in PNG and SVG formats. Publication Tables 5–8 in CSV format. Source cross-validation results and record-level predictions. Ottawa classification scores, calibration results, and decision thresholds. Group-based bootstrap results and supporting feature statistics. Experimental protocol, raw-data checksums, software environment information, and reproducibility verification reports. Numerical results were checked against the manuscript at the reported precision. The archive also includes independent verification of metrics recalculated from serialized prediction files. The original raw vibration recordings are not redistributed. They remain accessible through the original dataset repositories. Original datasets: MCC5–THU: https://doi.org/10.17632/6s3dggj9mw.1 University of Ottawa Electric Motor Dataset: https://doi.org/10.17632/msxs4vj48g.2 This repository supports transparent evaluation, independent verification, and reproducibility of the reported experimental findings.

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into online language teaching has gained increasing attention due to its potential to enhance instructional efficiency, provide real-time feedback, and support personalized learning in EFL contexts. However, previous research has typically focused on teachers’ perceptions, readiness or challenges in using AI separately from one another, resulting in a fragmented picture of AI adoption. The present study investigates EFL teachers’ understanding of AI, the context-specific variables affecting their readiness for deploying it, and the barriers to incorporating it in online language teaching. Using semi-structured interviews with nine EFL teachers, a qualitative case study design was used, and analysis of the data was by means of thematic methods. Drawing upon the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, the study aims to understand teachers’ adoption and integration of AI Tools. The results show that teachers tend to perceive AI as a learning assistant and efficiency-oriented tool, which represents autonomous and flexible modes of learning. However, several barriers persist, including limited conceptual understanding of AI, difficulties in selecting appropriate tools, pedagogical and ethical concerns regarding student over-reliance and academic integrity, and technical constraints. The study highlights important pedagogical implications, suggesting the need for targeted professional development, clearer instructional guidelines, and institutional support to promote effective and responsible AI integration in EFL classrooms.

The advent of generative AI has provoked an ontological crisis in language education, tempting policymakers to equate machine-generated output with human interpretive capacity. This article challenges the premise that such technologies render language learning obsolete, arguing instead that an AI-saturated landscape makes robust humanistic engagement more vital than ever. Addressing the “scholar’s dilemma,” the paper proposes a structural shift in higher education from traditional silos toward horizontal, cross-disciplinary integration. Because English functions as a global lingua franca (ELF) and exerts an algorithmic hegemony over large language models (LLMs), advanced proficiency remains indispensable for critically querying these platforms. We advocate for a pedagogical evolution from the mechanical transmission of referential information (informing) to facilitating imaginative exploration (engaging). Central to this shift is the reclamation of “literature with a small l” as the primary representational material used to cultivate students’ “textual power.” By prioritizing the interpretive struggle over cognitive offloading—a tension described here as the “Picasso Paradox”—educators can formalize a “fifth skill” (complex critical thinking in English). This framework provides the cognitive foundation for students to navigate an AI-saturated world not as passive users, but as active curators equipped with ethical discernment and epistemic agency.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate other models’ outputs in medicine, an approach known as LLM-as-a-Judge (LaaJ), yet no LaaJ-specific reporting checklist exists. This scoping review included 91 medical LaaJ studies: 69 from 5,571 database records and 22 from a previous review. Judges were mainly used for response evaluation (74.7%), and 76.9% of the studies used at least one proprietary LLM. Agreement with human evaluators was reported in 65.9% of the studies, with widely varying metrics. Based on these findings, this study developed RULE-LLM, a reporting framework of 21 items and eight sub-items across four domains: role and task specification, underlying data and criteria, LLM-Judge design and output, and evaluation of judge performance. Seven experts rated the initial draft (S-CVI/Ave, 0.94), and five independent raters showed substantial agreement when applying the final framework (Fleiss' κ, 0.67; Gwet's AC1, 0.73). RULE-LLM aims to improve the transparency and reproducibility of LaaJ studies.

documents.abstract: The rapid expansion of app-based food delivery has intensified concerns about riders’ road safety and occupational health. This scoping review maps and synthesises existing research on the safety of food delivery riders, including its methodological characteristics, multilevel determinants, safety and health outcomes, and prevention approaches. Following the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews, Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, and TRID were searched for English-language sources published from 2013 to 2026. After duplicate removal and two stage screening, 198 sources were included and synthesised through descriptive mapping and thematic analysis. The evidence comprised surveys, interviews, observations, naturalistic riding studies, platform data, and retrospective hospital and crash records. The evidence base was dominated by cross-sectional and self-reported research. Research activity in this field surged from 2022. Findings indicate that rider safety and health are shaped by interacting determinants at four levels: individual characteristics; work and platform conditions; road, vehicle, and environmental conditions; and institutional and social protection. Reported outcomes extended beyond risky riding, crashes, and traffic injuries to include musculoskeletal symptoms, fatigue, sleep disturbance, environmental exposure, and psychological distress. Only a small proportion of studies evaluated implemented interventions, leaving the effectiveness of platform, infrastructure, and policy level measures uncertain. Current evidence remains geographically concentrated, methodologically heterogeneous, and limited in its capacity to establish causal relationships. Improving rider safety therefore requires a shared, systems-based approach involving riders, platforms, restaurants, customers, transport authorities, and labour regulators, alongside longitudinal, exposure-adjusted, and intervention focused research.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Science communication leverages online multimedia to raise public awareness of research and discovery, yet its efficacy is built upon digital competencies, communication and storytelling. These skills sit outside the scope of traditional scientific training, and artificial intelligence (AI) tools can accelerate professional learning in service of public outreach. Three different AI prompting strategies were used to convert a research article written by the author to a format appropriate for a public lecture. Different titles, graphics, and a talk outline informed by the Three Act Storytelling framework were extracted from the paper using one-shot, chain of thought and role-prompting strategies. These resources can be re-purposed for video abstracts, lay summaries and social media posts to facilitate science communication to a broad generalist audience. The effectiveness of AI as a collaborative tool for ideation is considered alongside its impact on scientific credibility and graduate employability.

Education 5.0 places human agency, ethical technology use, critical thinking, creativity, and meaningful learning at the centre of digital transformation. In higher education, this shift requires institutions to develop not only technological infrastructure but also the research and information literacies needed to evaluate AI-mediated knowledge. Scite.ai is an AI-enabled scholarly citation-intelligence platform that extends conventional citation indexing by displaying citation context and classifying citation statements as supporting, contrasting, or mentioning. This chapter critically examines how Scite can contribute to AI readiness, research literacy, evidence evaluation, and responsible academic practice within an Education 5.0 ecosystem. An integrative review approach is used to synthesize Scite-specific research with literature on Education 5.0, AI literacy, information literacy, technology acceptance, human-centred AI, academic integrity, and institutional governance. The chapter argues that Scite should not be positioned as an automated authority or replacement for scholarly reading. Rather, it can function as an evidence-navigation and critical-reading layer within a broader institutional learning ecosystem. A new institutional conceptual framework is proposed in which Education 5.0 provides the normative context; institutional and stakeholder readiness provide enabling conditions; technology acceptance influences use; Scite-supported practices provide research affordances; and AI literacy, information literacy, critical evaluation, and evidence synthesis mediate potential outcomes. The framework is operationalized through a six-stage institutional roadmap: diagnose, prepare, pilot, integrate, evaluate, and scale. The chapter also identifies risks related to classification error, incomplete coverage, contextual ambiguity, automation bias, privacy, affordability, and academic integrity. The central conclusion is that the educational value of Scite depends less on automation itself than on the quality of human-AI interaction, pedagogical design, verification practices, and institutional governance surrounding its use.

Introduction: Mobile pre-hospital care plays a fundamental role in emergency and urgent healthcare assistance, being responsible for rapid and decisive interventions in life-threatening situations. In this context, health professionals working in Mobile Intensive Care Units are constantly exposed to different occupational risks, including biological, physical, ergonomic and psychosocial hazards resulting from the dynamic and unpredictable conditions of the work environment. Objective: To analyze the factors related to the safety of health professionals working in mobile pre-hospital care, with emphasis on occupational risks present in Mobile Intensive Care Units. Methodology: This is an integrative literature review, with a descriptive character and qualitative approach, carried out in the databases Virtual Health Library, LILACS, BDENF, SciELO and PubMed/MEDLINE. Full scientific articles published between 2020 and 2025, in Portuguese, English and Spanish, related to the proposed theme, were included. Results and Discussions: The analyzed studies showed that professionals working in mobile pre-hospital care are frequently exposed to accidents involving biological material, urban violence, traffic accidents, physical exhaustion, emotional overload and high levels of occupational stress. Furthermore, inadequate working conditions, insufficient material resources and limitations related to continuous training contribute to increasing the occupational vulnerability of these teams. On the other hand, the studies highlighted the importance of biosafety measures, proper use of Personal Protective Equipment, continuing education and strengthening institutional policies aimed at workers' health. Final considerations: It is concluded that occupational risks present in mobile pre-hospital care directly impact the health and quality of life of professionals, highlighting the need to strengthen protection strategies and occupational health promotion in urgent and emergency healthcare services.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence transforms self-correction from a localized answer-revision problem into a system-level reliability and recovery challenge. In autonomous, stateful, and long-horizon systems, early errors can propagate through reasoning, planning, retrieval, tool use, external actions, multi-agent interaction, and persistent memory. However, existing research often treats self-correction as either response-level refinement or a capability within broader agent architectures. This study develops an agent-level perspective that connects these fragmented views. It distinguishes reasoning, reflection, verification, correction, and adaptation, emphasizing that reasoning or critique alone does not constitute self-correction unless evaluative information produces a subsequent behavioral change. The study introduces a unified corrective lifecycle covering anomaly detection, error diagnosis and localization, corrective evidence acquisition, repair, validation, commitment or rollback, memory updating, and continuation, termination, or escalation. Existing approaches are organized across five dimensions: correction target, feedback source, temporal scope, persistence, and control architecture. A comparative synthesis shows that self-correction is not uniformly beneficial: repeated reflection can improve performance, stagnate, or degrade initially correct behavior. More reliable gains generally arise when feedback is task-relevant, informative, and at least partially independent of the process that produced the error. The study also identifies key failure modes, including missed errors, unsuccessful repair, over-correction, error amplification, memory contamination, and objective misalignment. These findings motivate research on calibrated intervention, memory integrity, verification, rollback, cost-aware correction, human escalation, and resilience under distribution shift.

Basketball play-by-play data provide semi-structured descriptions of game events, but connecting analytical queries to the corresponding moments in broadcast video remains challenging. Towards this direction, this paper presents a semantic framework that integrates basketball play-by-play information into a Knowledge Graph (KG) through the BBall ontology, and links recorded events to temporally grounded video segments using scoreboard-based optical character recognition (OCR). The framework supports multimodal exploitation using structured queries over game events, through the research prototype CourtLens. The latter enables users to retrieve relevant video evidence through a unified semantic interface, including interactive shot charts, filters, SPARQL queries, and natural-language questions through LLM-to-SPARQL. The underlying KG contains 9.5 M play-by-play-related triples covering 1063 games, while the interactive video catalogue currently provides synchronized access to 28 games from 3 EuroLeague seasons. Concerning evaluation, a manually annotated benchmark of 1833 actions from three EuroLeague games yields an overall median absolute temporal error of 4.0 s, with 57.72% and 68.46% of all actions localized within 5 s and 10 s, respectively. Notably, running-clock events (missed/made field goals, assists, rebounds, blocks, steals and turnovers) achieve higher accuracy with 81.04% localized within 5 s and 90.47% within 10 s, demonstrating the system’s effectiveness in temporally grounding actions during active gameplay. Finally, the offline grounding pipeline processes video at 22.74× real time, whereas the interactive CourtLens web application offers real-time interaction for video analysis, e.g., less than 1 s for filter-based search.

Longitudinal computational psychiatry aims to build computer models that track how a person's hidden mental health state changes over time using incomplete real-world clues like daily symptoms, behavior, physical data, and environment. While standard time-series models are great for tracking changing systems, they often break down when the number of hidden variables is large, measurements are missing, and different types of uncertainty overlap. This paper introduces a new method to estimate these hidden states cleanly and efficiently by breaking down complex updates into a sequence of simple, structured approximations.What Problem This SolvesTracking hidden mental states: In psychiatry, clinicians cannot directly measure a patient's underlying neurobiological or psychological state. Instead, models must infer these hidden states from indirect signals like smartphone usage, heart rate, sleep patterns, and self-reported mood.Handling messy, high-dimensional data: Real-world patient data is often incomplete, noisy, and spans many interacting variables. Updating a model's estimate of a patient's state when new data arrives requires complex calculations that become slow and unreliable as the number of variables grows.Borrowing from data compression: The authors adapt a technique originally designed for compressing images in generative AI. Instead of compressing pixels, they use the same logic to compress and simplify the adjustments a model makes when updating its belief about a patient's mental state.How the Sequential Codebook Method WorksDefining the update target: Whenever new patient data arrives, the model needs to adjust its previous estimate of the patient's hidden state. This adjustment is called the posterior state correction, and the goal is to approximate it using a limited, efficient amount of information.Building a menu of candidate updates: Rather than searching through infinite possibilities to fix its estimate, the model generates several independent "sections," or groups, of random candidate adjustments. Each candidate is shaped to respect the natural correlations and uncertainty patterns among the patient's hidden variables.Picking the best match step by step: In the first section, the model compares all available candidates against the current estimation error (the residual) and picks the single candidate that aligns best with what needs to be fixed. It then subtracts that adjustment and moves to the next section to fix whatever error remains.Predictable error reduction: Under ideal conditions, the authors prove that each sequential step reduces the remaining estimation error by a reliable, predictable fraction. Because each section works independently on the leftover error, adding more sections steadily shrinks the overall mistake at a guaranteed rate.Accounting for real-world digital limits: In theory, the weight given to each chosen candidate could be any continuous number. In practice, computers must round these weights to finite digital values (quantization), so the authors explicitly calculate how this rounding affects accuracy.Real-World Extensions and SafeguardsHandling missing data and shifting conditions: Longitudinal studies frequently suffer from missed check-ins or dead wearable batteries. The framework is expanded to handle missing data types and to remain accurate even when a patient's data patterns shift away from what the model originally expected.Clear rules and failure modes: The authors lay out the exact conditions required for their error-reduction guarantees to hold. They also examine when the model might fail or struggle to tell two different hidden causes apart (identifiability).A roadmap for testing: The authors emphasize that this framework is a proposed research method, not a ready-to-use clinical tool. To prove its worth, it must be tested on unseen patient data, checked for reliable uncertainty estimates, stripped down to test which parts actually matter, and compared directly against traditional tracking models.Core TakeawayBridging statistics and state estimation: The paper's main theoretical breakthrough is linking the statistics of extreme values in random bell-curve samples (Gaussian order statistics) to step-by-step error reduction. This provides a mathematically grounded way to update complex, uncertainty-weighted models of human mental health.

documents.abstract: Authority Files in the Age of AI: Building Trustworthy Information Through Collaboration As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes how we conduct research and retrieve information, the need for trustworthy and reliable information has never been greater. Authority files have long played a vital role in improving precision and recall in information retrieval, traditionally in bibliographic catalogues and increasingly in research data as well. But what potential do they hold for AI applications, and how can they help ensure that AI systems provide reliable information? This presentation explores the role of authority files as a foundation for trustworthy AI applications. It highlights the importance of bringing together the knowledge and expertise of diverse communities to create a broader and more inclusive network of reference entities – without compromising the reliability and quality of the data. Using the cooperative framework of the Gemeinsame Normdatei (GND) as an example, the presentation introduces an integrative infrastructure that enables communities to contribute their expertise to the collaborative creation and maintenance of authority data. Discover how collaboration, shared expertise and reliable authority data can help shape a more trustworthy information landscape in the age of AI. documents.abstract: Modern artificial intelligence paradigm designs overwhelmingly prioritize performance metrics, optimization velocity, and computational efficiency, reducing human oversight to post-hoc compliance mechanisms. This paper presents Sittisart (Rights-Centric Framework), a governance standard engineered to re-establish human sovereignty as the primary, non-negotiable axiom of artificial intelligence architecture. Sittisart posits that human autonomy over personal data, context interpretation, and final decision-making must structurally precede algorithmic performance. We articulate a Four-Layer Rights Architecture (R1–R4)—comprising Data Sovereignty, Consent Integrity, Interpretation Rights, and the Right to Cut—complemented by Three System Integrity Laws. Together, these frameworks define verifiable operational boundaries that prevent opaque inference, silent profiling, and semantic collapse in intelligent systems, establishing a standardized blueprint for privacy-preserving, human-aligned AI deployment.

Background/Objectives: Video-assisted CPR (V-CPR) improves the quality of CPR. Nevertheless, the available evidence has focused primarily on adult cardiac arrest scenarios and on compression-dominated resuscitation manoeuvres. In the paediatric setting, where ventilation is critical, the usefulness of V-CPR has scarcely been explored. We aimed to compare V-CPR using smartglasses and/or smartphones with each other and with voice-only assistance via smartphone in a simulated paediatric cardiac arrest. Methods: In this experimental pilot simulation study, thirty-four undergraduate sports science students without BLS training in the previous two years participated in a simulated cardiac arrest of an 8-year-old child, under dispatcher guidance. Participants received video-assistance using smartglasses (VA-SG), video-assistance using a smartphone (VA-Ph), or voice-only assistance (C). They performed 5 min of CPR (30:2 ratio). Assessments included CPR quality, response times, and CPR skills. Results: We showed that VA-Ph and VA-SG outperformed C in most outcomes. Significant differences were observed in the number of effective ventilations (p = 0.010) and chest compressions (CC) at correct depth (p = 0.006). Ventilation quality was 37.1 ± 32.9% in C, 70.1 ± 30.7% in VA-Ph, and 66.3 ± 28.9% in VA-SG (p = 0.038). CC quality reached 55.6 ± 28.0% in C, 74.0 ± 22.9% in VA-Ph, and 77.9 ± 16.6% in VA-SG (p = 0.150). Overall CPR quality was numerically higher in both video-assisted groups, although the difference was not statistically significant. V-CPR also improved correct CC hand placement (p = 0.001) and airway opening (p = 0.036). Response times did not differ significantly between groups. Conclusions: Video-assistance via smartglasses or smartphones improves key components of the quality of dispatcher-guided CPR during simulated paediatric cardiac arrest, doubling effective ventilations and improving the proportion of compressions at correct depth, with no significant differences in time to CPR initiation. Direct scene visualisation gives dispatchers better situational awareness, enabling more accurate, real-time guidance that could translate into higher-quality resuscitation and improved outcomes.

documents.abstract: Socioeconomic differences in adolescents’ school belonging and school loneliness are important concerns for psychological adjustment. As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into schoolwork, its associations with students’ school experiences and the moderating roles of relational resources warrant examination. This study used cross-sectional PISA data from adolescents in four Chinese regions. Unweighted multiple linear regression analyses examined economic, social and cultural status (ESCS) and AI use for schoolwork in relation to school loneliness and school belonging. Family support and peer academic help-seeking were examined separately as moderators of the associations between ESCS and each outcome. All models included sex, age, and school fixed effects. Multiple testing was addressed using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure. Higher ESCS and more frequent AI use for schoolwork were associated with lower school loneliness and greater school belonging. Peer academic help-seeking moderated the association between ESCS and school loneliness after FDR correction. The negative association weakened as peer academic help-seeking increased. Family support did not significantly moderate either association, and peer academic help-seeking did not significantly moderate the association between ESCS and school belonging. These findings suggest a limited compensatory role for peer academic help-seeking in socioeconomic differences in school loneliness, providing partial support for the resource compensation perspective.

Soil salinity is one of the major environmental constraints limiting agricultural productivity and global food security, affecting approximately 833 M ha of land worldwide. Its extent is increasing due to climate change, seawater intrusion, rock weathering, poor irrigation practices, inadequate drainage, groundwater over-extraction, excessive fertiliser use, irrigation with saline water and industrial effluent discharge. Salinity degrades soil structure, reduces nutrient availability, impairs photosynthesis, restricts plant growth and ultimately decreases crop productivity. This review provides a comprehensive and up-to-date synthesis of the causes, impacts, assessment methods and management strategies for soil salinity while highlighting recent advances in biotechnology and precision agriculture. Unlike previous reviews that focus on individual aspects of salinity, this review integrates conventional and emerging approaches within a single framework. Relevant literature was systematically identified and screened using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) methodology to ensure transparent and comprehensive coverage. Recent advances in salinity assessment include remote sensing, electromagnetic induction (EMI), machine learning and geospatial techniques, enabling accurate large-scale monitoring and management of salt-affected soils. Effective mitigation strategies include improved irrigation and drainage, mulching, chemical amendments, silicon (Si) application, beneficial microorganisms, phytoremediation, nanotechnology and integrated soil management. Biotechnological approaches such as marker-assisted breeding, molecular breeding and CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing have accelerated the development of salt-tolerant crop varieties, including BRRI dhan73, BRRI dhan99, CSR 101 and CSR 104. Future research should prioritise climate-resilient agriculture, sustainable land reclamation, precision farming and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven technologies to enhance long-term salinity management and food security.

Shoreline management in the Western Indian Ocean (WIO) is largely informed by small-scale studies with coarse temporal resolution, potentially obscuring fine spatial patterns and interannual dynamics. This study examines spatiotemporal shoreline change along 400 km of the Kenyan coastline from 2000 to 2024 and tests its association with regional sea-level trend and variability, accounting for spatial dependence. Twenty-five annual Landsat-derived shoreline positions were analyzed using the Digital Shoreline Analysis System (DSAS) along 12,455 transects using Weighted Linear Regression (WLR) weighted by a tide- and registration-based positional uncertainty of approximately 40 to 68 m per epoch. Sea-level predictors were derived from GLORYS12V1 reanalysis at its native grid (47 coastal cells) and tested with Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), a Spatial Lag Model (SLM), and Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR). Results reveal pronounced spatial heterogeneity. The Kilifi and Kwale–Mombasa zones show net accretion (mean WLR 0.57 and 0.51 m yr -1 , respectively), whereas the Tana–Manda zone shows net erosion (mean WLR = −0.92 m yr −1 ), with 36.23% of its transects significantly eroding. The national mean Net Shoreline Movement of +9.45 m obscures this variability. Shoreline change is strongly spatially autocorrelated (Moran’s I = 0.866, p = 0.001) and 12.01% of transects form statistically significant local clusters (6.23% as High–High accretion and 5.57% Low–Low erosion clusters). Neither sea-level trend nor sea-level variability showed a detectable association with shoreline change at the native support of the predictors (OLS R 2 ≤ 0.028, p ≥ 0.26; SLM not significant; GWR adjusted R 2 < 0). At the scales resolved here, shoreline change along the Kenyan coast is therefore not explained by regional sea-level variation and is more plausibly linked to local geomorphic and human factors. National averages must be complemented by spatially explicit, uncertainty-weighted assessments to inform shoreline management policy.

Autonomous AI agents increasingly decompose user instructions into task lists, but widely used approaches (AutoGPT, BabyAGI, MetaGPT) generate simple linear, ID-ordered sequences that cannot express conditional branching or parallel execution. Newer orchestration frameworks such as LangGraph, the LLM Compiler, and the Claude Agent SDK add DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) or state-machine execution control for non-linear workflows, yet none provides a quantitative, probabilistic estimate of how likely a plan is to succeed, or how much a redundant (alternative) path improves that likelihood. This study integrates DAG-based dependency modeling, prompt engineering for conditional branching, and a state-machine execution engine, and formulates the resulting task-completion probability P(Goal) with reliability engineering. The model is generalized to 1-out-of-n (parallel) path redundancy and to general DAG topologies with parallel branching and AND-joins, and a cost-constrained redundancy-allocation problem and a Beta-prior estimator of path success probabilities from execution logs are given. Assuming independent task outcomes, Monte Carlo simulations (10,000–100,000 trials) of a retrieval-and-summarization task (72.7% completion for the linear model, 84.4% with redundancy) agree with the closed-form predictions to within 0.18 percentage points across 24 parameter combinations and within 1 point under all conditions. Redundancy at the bottleneck stage yields about 3.9 times the gain at the most reliable stage, as the marginal-utility formula predicts. Alternative paths help most when failures are persistent; correlated failures reduce the gain. With a real LLM agent (100 runs), completion rates predicted from probabilities estimated on half the runs fell within the 95% intervals observed on the other half.

Teachers increasingly use generative artificial intelligence to prepare lessons, yet few accounts describe how teachers who are comfortable with digital tools do this successfully, what they still need, and how this looks in Philippine schools. This study documented the experiences of tech-savvy teachers in crafting lesson plans with artificial intelligence, the digital competencies they credited for their success, the challenges and strategies they reported, and the institutional support they recommended. A qualitative exploratory-descriptive design was used. Fifteen teachers of languages, mathematics, social science and social studies, organization and management, and agriculture, with 1 year 8 months to 16 years of teaching experience, were recruited through convenience and referral sampling and answered an online open-ended questionnaire. Tool use was summarized with frequencies and percentages, and the 58 written responses were analyzed through thematic analysis. ChatGPT (80%) and Google Gemini (66.7%) were the most used tools. Four themes emerged. First, fourteen teachers described planning with artificial intelligence as faster, easier, and more productive, and two noted effort at the outset, mainly in writing prompts. Second, success was linked to foundational digital literacy, prompt writing, and the ability to evaluate output, used together with teaching judgment. Third, the main challenges were output that did not fit learners, inaccurate information, and over-reliance, which teachers managed by reviewing, verifying, and localizing output. Fourth, teachers asked for continuous training, peer collaboration, and clear guidelines on appropriate use and its declaration. Interpreted through the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge framework and technology acceptance theory, the findings suggest that these teachers’ success rested on their own judgment, prompting skill, and the support available to them. Because of the small sample, the brevity of many responses, and signs that some responses were machine-assisted, the findings are exploratory and not generalizable.

Sustainability-oriented entrepreneurship education is gaining traction, but few studies examine the mechanisms by which learning experiences translate into intentions to create socially and environmentally responsible businesses. Based on Human Capital Theory and the Theory of Planned Behaviour, this research investigates the mediating effect of sustainable opportunity recognition and green creativity sequentially and the moderating effect of Generative AI Literacy for Learning. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) was used to analyse the survey responses of 407 students from public and private universities in Punjab, Pakistan. The findings showed a positive correlation between educational exposure and opportunity identification, which is linked to creative idea generation and, in turn, higher entrepreneurial intentions. The indirect (sequential) relationship is significant. Moreover, GenAI literacy strengthens both the education–intention and creativity–intention relationships, suggesting that technological competence complements sustainability-focused learning. These findings complement the existing explanations of entrepreneurial intention by adding an extension of the cognitive and creative process to a technology-related boundary condition. The study also underscores the importance of integrating sustainability problems, opportunities, innovative problem-solving, and responsible leveraging of generative AI into the curriculum, especially for higher education institutions, which are crucial for nurturing entrepreneurial aspirations in today's learning landscape.

This study aims to examine the challenges, implementation strategies, and benefits of integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into vocational education and practice from 2021 to 2025. A systematic literature review was conducted using the PRISMA approach. Data were collected from the Scopus database. A Total of 17 articles met the inclusion criteria and then were analyzed using the PICOC framework. Findings indicate that the adoption of AI in vocational education and training not only faces technical issues but also challenges related to human readiness, institutional capacity, digital literacy, infrastructure gaps, and unequal access between developed and developing countries. Effective AI implementation requires an integrated strategy involving adaptive curriculum design, continuous training for educators, institutional leadership, industry collaboration, and the development of a supportive digital ecosystem. The integration of AI offers significant benefits in enhancing the quality of learning, the effectiveness of training, competency alignment, and workplace readiness, but its impact depends on how well the technology aligns with pedagogy, institutional readiness, and industry needs. Overall, the success of AI integration cannot be measured only by the technology used, but also by the capabilities of educational institutions and the creation of a collaborative ecosystem that is valuable to industry.

documents.abstract: With the large-scale implementation of generative artificial intelligence, digital twin, BIM and other technologies in the construction industry, the construction industry is transforming from the traditional manual construction mode to the intelligent construction mode, and the demand for industry post ability has changed significantly. As a core compulsory course of civil engineering undergraduate major, civil engineering construction undertakes the task of imparting professional knowledge such as construction technology, construction organization and site management. The traditional classroom teaching mode has practical contradictions such as lack of practical scenes, lagging update of teaching content, insufficient individualized training of students, and single assessment method. The teaching practice shows that the reasonable introduction of AI auxiliary tools can make up for the shortcomings of traditional teaching field conditions, enrich classroom case resources, and strengthen students’ engineering practice thinking. However, it also faces practical challenges such as students’ excessive dependence on AI output content, professional information distortion, and teachers’ teaching ability can not keep up with technical iteration. This study can provide reference for the digital teaching reform of construction courses in similar engineering majors, and help to cultivate compound civil engineering talents with both traditional construction skills and intelligent construction literacy.

Banks in emerging economies are under pressure to deliver faster, more personalised and more efficient digital financial services, yet many struggle to convert investments in artificial intelligence (AI) into innovation. This study examined how two dimensions of AI adoption readiness, technological readiness and organisational readiness, relate to product innovation and process innovation in deposit money banks in Yenagoa, Bayelsa State, Nigeria. Anchored on the Technology Acceptance Model and the Resource-Based View, the study adopted a descriptive, cross-sectional, correlational survey of 400 employees and managers selected through stratified random sampling. Data were analysed with descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple regression. Respondents rated organisational readiness (M = 3.62), process innovation (M = 3.59), product innovation (M = 3.54) and technological readiness (M = 3.45) above the scale midpoint. Both readiness dimensions correlated strongly and positively with both innovation outcomes (r = .68 to .74, p < .001). In multiple regression, the two predictors jointly explained 57.5% of the variance in product innovation and 56.7% in process innovation, and organisational readiness had the larger standardised coefficient in both models (β = .535 and .444) compared with technological readiness (β = .263 and .353). The findings indicate that technology is necessary but not sufficient for AI-enabled innovation. Banks should pair investment in infrastructure and skills with leadership sponsorship, employee training, a supportive culture and strategic alignment.

Context: The acceleration of digital transformation has reshaped learning environments in higher education and the conditions under which teachers and students engage in the learning process. This transformation creates opportunities while also posing challenges related to digital competencies, equity, and technological governance. Objective: To analyze the opportunities, challenges, and educational trends associated with the use of digital technologies in higher education. Method: A systematic literature review was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines and the Population, Interest, and Context (PICo) framework. Searches were performed in Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, SciELO, ERIC, and Dialnet. The final corpus comprised 25 empirical studies published between 2022 and September 2026. Results: The findings identified learning flexibility and personalization, the early adoption of generative artificial intelligence, and the growing importance of teachers' digital competence as major educational trends. Disparities in access were also observed, influenced by technological infrastructure and training opportunities. Blended learning and ethical technology governance emerged as key elements in guiding institutional transformation. Conclusions: The effective pedagogical integration of digital technologies in higher education requires coherent institutional policies, continuous professional development for faculty members, and critical digital literacy across the university community. Technological transformation must be accompanied by strategies aimed at narrowing digital access gaps and ensuring educational integration that is contextually relevant, equitable, and responsible.

Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has become an important area of research as AI systems are increasingly used to support cybersecurity decisions. Providing explanations for AI-generated recommendations can improve transparency, help users understand system outputs, and support greater confidence in automated decisions. However, increasing the amount of information provided by an AI system may also create additional cognitive demands for users, particularly when explanations contain complex technical information. This paper examines the AI explainability paradox in cybersecurity, focusing on the relationship between explanation complexity, cognitive load, human understanding, and security decision-making. Drawing on existing literature related to explainable AI, cognitive load, human-AI interaction, cybersecurity decision-making, and technology trust, the paper develops a conceptual framework linking AI explanation, information complexity, cognitive load, user understanding, verification behaviour, and decision quality. The paper proposes that effective explainability should not be determined only by the amount of information provided, but also by the ability of users to understand and effectively use that information during security-related decisions. While appropriate explanations may improve transparency and support informed judgement, excessive or technically complex explanations may increase cognitive load and reduce decision effectiveness. The proposed framework provides a foundation for future empirical research examining how different levels of AI explanation influence human cybersecurity decisions and contributes to the development of human-centred explainable AI systems.

Today, businesses are making more and more use of Artificial Intelligent (AI) technologies in their operations. This widespread use of AI technologies is changing how a consumer searches, evaluates and purchases products in the online intelligent markets. Consumer behavior is shaped by consumer’s own cognition as well as influence by machine learning systems (AI technologies). These advanced systems use algorithmic personalization, predictive analysis, ranking systems and automated decision support to guide the consumers. To understand the consumer buying behavior in these intelligent markets, this paper, titled “The Algorithmic Consumer: A Theoretical Perspective on Consumer Buying Behavior in Intelligent Markets,” proposes an integrated conceptual framework. “Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) (Venkatesh et al. 2003)”, “Diffusion of Innovations (Rogers, 2003)” and “Disruptive Innovation Perspectives (Christensen, 1997)” are the foundations of this research. This paper argues that the algorithmic influence works through three interconnected mechanisms namely, behavioral reinforcement through personalization, cognitive effort reduction and perceived performance enhancement. Here, conventional consumer behavior models are extended by adding new constructs such as algorithmic trust, perceived AI transparency, adaptive habit formation and data-driven social influence. This paper proposes that AI tools and systems do not simply play the role of marketing tools but also actively influence consumer preferences, attention, post-purchase learning and habits. In this work, theory is being built methodologically and conceptual synthesis technique is used. Model abstraction (simplification) and comparison analysis is used to achieve proposed conceptual integration. A through multidisciplinary analysis which included literature from marketing, information systems and innovation studies, was carried out. The aim of this exercise was to identify overlapping theoretical frameworks. With this exercise a nested framework is created that connect behavioral results, psychological mediators and technology affordances. Traditional consumer theories have been used, which focus on the human-centric framework as a base for this exercise. This base was further expanded to understand AI-augmented viewpoint. This study strongly proposes that AI tools & systems are actively involved in the consumer’s decisions-making journey as opposed to the previous conception of them being simply passive actors, guiding consumers. The implications of this study highlight that organizations must manage system transparency, trust alignment and personalization to maximize consumer engagement. This study describes “algorithmic consumer” and its inception. Going further, this study also lays foundation for future empirical studies as well as policy discussions of autonomy, ethics, and control over pricing in the AI-powered digital ecosystems.

Objective: This study aims to develop an artificial intelligence (AI) system based on the U-Net deep learning architecture to automatically identify and stage lymphatic vessels in indocyanine green (ICG) lymphography images, thereby enhancing recognition efficiency and objectivity and assisting in the planning of lymphaticovenular anastomosis (LVA) surgery. Methods: A total of 560 ICG lymphography images from 140 patients with lower-limb lymphedema were collected. After standard preprocessing, the images were randomly split into a training set and a test set in a 7:3 ratio. The U-Net model was used for training, with hyperparameters optimized using a five-fold cross-validation approach. The Adam optimizer was employed for model training. Evaluation metrics included precision, recall, F1 score, and inference time. Results: The model demonstrated excellent performance in identifying lymphatic vessels across lymphedema stages I–IV. The precision scores for each stage were as follows: stage I: 95.29%, stage II: 92.58%, stage III: 93.17%, and stage IV: 90.08%. Recall rates for all stages were above 89%, and all F1 scores exceeded 90%, indicating strong overall accuracy and balance between precision and recall. The average inference time per image was just 56 milliseconds, highlighting the model’s suitability for near-real-time applications. Additionally, the confusion matrix revealed a high discriminative capability across the different lymphedema stages. Conclusion: The U-Net-based AI model demonstrated high accuracy and efficiency in the automatic identification of lymphatic vessels in ICG images, highlighting its strong potential for clinical applications. This system may significantly support LVA surgical planning, enable real-time intraoperative navigation, and serve as a valuable tool for physician training.

Research on construction digitalisation has grown quickly but remains fragmented. This narrative review examines Scopus-indexed journal articles published between 2016 and 2025 on Building Information Modelling (BIM), artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, digital twins and related automation. A pool of 494 records was screened by title, abstract and keywords, and 89 articles were retained. An eligibility audit then separated 78 core studies from 11 records in which digital technology was contextual. The review combines a descriptive profile of the literature with an explicit, criteria based assessment of evidence maturity and of circular economy linkage. This narrative review used a single database and screening by one reviewer. Exclusion followed a construct based relevance test and not study quality. The exact date of the Scopus search was not recorded. Output accelerated after 2022 (74.2% of the 89 articles appeared from 2023 to 2025), 77.5% appeared in two MDPI journals, and author affiliations were concentrated in China and the United Kingdom. Nine overlapping themes emerged, led by BIM for design, coordination and compliance (39 core studies), robotics, automation and additive manufacturing (30), and AI and machine learning (24). Six records addressed circularity or waste reduction, and only two applied a digital tool to a material recovery or waste outcome. Within the retrieved sample, the link to the circular economy is therefore a thin evidence base and not an established finding, and the low count may partly reflect the search strategy. Case studies, pilots and cross sectional surveys are common (19 and 16 of the 89 screened records, respectively), whereas longitudinal studies and multisite validation appear limited. Blockchain evidence in the sample is minimal. A research agenda is proposed for validated, integrated and context-sensitive studies.

Generative artificial intelligence has destabilised an assumption embedded in copyright doctrine: that the person who communicates instructions to a machine is also the person who creates the resulting expression. This article examines where Sri Lankan copyright law should draw the line between AI-generated and AI-assisted literary and artistic works. Employing doctrinal and comparative methods, it analyses the Intellectual Property Act, No. 36 of 2003, leading Sri Lankan originality decisions and approaches adopted in the United States, the United Kingdom, the European Union and India. It argues that the statutory requirement of a physical-person author prevents attribution of authorship to an autonomous system, but does not preclude protection for sufficiently original human contributions embodied in an AI-mediated work. It proposes a five-stage Human Creative Contribution Test, proceeding through attribution, expressive specification, effective control and causation, originality, and protection and allocation. The proposed model avoids both automatic copyright for every prompt and indiscriminate denial of protection whenever AI has assisted a human creator. It further recommends evidential disclosure, clarification of partial protection and carefully framed statutory guidance rather than the immediate introduction of machine authorship.

Trust in artificial intelligence systems has become increasingly important as these systems assume advisory and decision-support roles. The present studies examine whether the temporal presentation of artificial intelligence (AI) generated responses, specifically typing animation speed, affects trust in chat-based interfaces. In Experiment 1, participants ( N = 71) interacted with three AI agents using pre-scripted question-response pairs detailing different facts about exotic animals. Response presentation speed (slow, fast, or instant) was manipulated within subjects. Results showed that compared to instant presentation, typing animations significantly increased trust in the AI agent but not trust in individual responses. Experiment 2 ( N = 68) employed similar procedures but used a live language model and allowed participants to generate their own questions. Under these more naturalistic conditions, presentation speed influenced both measures of trust, with typing animations consistently producing higher trust than instant presentation. These findings demonstrate that temporal presentation features can systematically shape trust judgments independent of content quality.

Generative AI disclosure is commonly treated as a means of making manuscript production transparent. This article argues that its epistemic value is more limited. Authors may accurately report observable operations, retained outputs, and verification procedures, but functional labels such as “language polishing” or “idea generation” cannot fully reconstruct the causal contribution of AI to a finished manuscript. Nevertheless, such descriptions may strongly influence scholarly evaluation. To examine this asymmetry, the article develops the readerly distraction model, distinguishing justified provenance monitoring from disproportionate attention to features insufficiently related to the disclosed operation. Readerly distraction is analytically distinct from evaluative stigma, although disproportionate monitoring may contribute to negative perceptions of originality, competence, or trustworthiness. The model generates testable predictions concerning attention allocation, comprehension, and evaluation, including comparisons between AI assistance and functionally equivalent human mediation. The article further proposes epistemically proportionate reporting through three complementary categories: methodological reporting, governance reporting, and production-provenance disclosure. Reporting requirements should reflect the role of adopted outputs, their epistemic risks, and the procedures used to verify them rather than the quantity of AI involvement. Finally, the article develops accountable judgment as a standard of authorship comprising understanding, verification, decision authority, and answerability. Unlike nominal responsibility, accountable judgment requires capacities and procedures that can be examined when scholarly claims are challenged. Together, these proposals seek to preserve meaningful transparency without allowing speculative technological provenance to displace the evaluation of evidence and reasoning.

documents.abstract: This concept paper explores the evolution and integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) within foreign language education, specifically examining the transition from Computer-Assisted Language Learning (CALL) to Intelligent Computer-Assisted Language Learning (ICALL). Current research indicates that AI technologies, such as Machine Learning (ML) and Natural Language Processing (NLP), are being utilized to provide personalized learning experiences, automated feedback, and sophisticated assessment tools. While these tools demonstrate significant pedagogical benefits, including improved language proficiency and increased learner autonomy, challenges remain regarding teacher preparation, technological reliability, and ethical implications. This paper proposes a framework to effectively integrate AI into pedagogy, repositioning the teacher as a facilitator and mentor in an AI-enhanced environment.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping manufacturing work, offering opportunities for employee empowerment while introducing psychological and organizational demands. Using selected PRISMA 2020 reporting items to describe search and study selection, this structured narrative review draws on a final corpus of 16 empirical studies to develop the Human–AI Resource Dynamics (HARD) framework, integrating Conservation of Resources (COR) theory and the Job Demands–Resources (JD–R) model. A theory-informed narrative synthesis identifies two potentially coexisting pathways with uneven empirical support. The Bright Empowering Path links psychological availability, self-efficacy, positive appraisals, and task fit with proactive behavior and performance. The proposed Dark Depleting Path organizes distinct associations involving hindrance appraisal, AI anxiety, job insecurity, and surveillance-related autonomy loss, rather than one empirically validated depletion chain. Individual, organizational, and technological conditions shape these relationships. Evidence for empowerment is comparatively more consistent, whereas depletion findings remain heterogeneous and primarily observational. Methodological diversity, geographical concentration, and limited longitudinal evidence constrain causal and cross-contextual conclusions. HARD provides an AI-specific integrative framework for future empirical testing and human-centered AI implementation within Industry 5.0.

Antibiotic-induced liver injury (AILI) is a heterogeneous subset of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) that ranges from self-limited biochemical abnormalities to acute liver failure and chronic cholestatic or autoimmune-like disease. This narrative review critically evaluates clinical and mechanistic evidence across major antibiotic classes while retaining a drug-centered structure. Human HLA associations, drug-specific T-cell responses, delayed onset, and immune-rich histology support adaptive immunity as a unifying framework for many therapeutic-dose idiosyncratic reactions. Direct evidence, however, varies by drug. Linezolid toxicity and historical high-dose intravenous tetracycline injury are better supported as non-idiosyncratic mitochondrial exceptions. Reactive metabolites, oxidative stress, transporter effects, and inflammatory stress may initiate or amplify injury, but cytotoxicity-only, lipopolysaccharide/TNF-α, animal, and organ-on-chip models do not by themselves reproduce clinical idiosyncratic AILI. In practice, management still requires phenotype classification, exclusion of competing causes, structured causality assessment, prompt withdrawal when feasible, severity-based referral, and avoidance of rechallenge. Biomarkers, pharmacogenomics, patient-specific models, microphysiological systems, and artificial intelligence remain investigational and require validation in adjudicated antibiotic-exposed cohorts with tolerant controls.

Police forces increasingly use Artificial Intelligence in support of specific tasks, such as data analysis, identifying suspects and monitoring public spaces. These uses potentially expand the state’s coercive capacity. Yet we know little about how far people accept these tools across political contexts and how these views systematically relate to other attitudes. We ask whether support rests on views of the technology, the problem AI use addresses, or trust in the institution using it. We analyze a preregistered survey of 9,000 respondents in the United States, China, Taiwan, the United Kingdom, and five EU countries using Bayesian multilevel models. Support is high for most uses everywhere. It rests on general AI benefits, perceived crime trends, and trust in the police, which matters similarly across countries. In contrast, general AI risks, personal fear of crime, and trust in legal institutions play no substantive role on average. Acceptance thus primarily is connected with optimism about AI, a general but not personal sense of problem relevance, and trust in the police.
