This essay argues that the phone and the computer will merge into a single device. Earlier attempts, phones that turn into a computer when plugged into a screen, changed how almost no one works, because the phone had to run desktop apps designed for a mouse and keyboard. The author argues that AI agents change this: once the heavy lifting is something you ask for in plain words, it no longer matters which device you speak from, and the merging of devices follows from a change in how people communicate with machines. Drawing on his own need to reach his agents from anywhere, and on the phone app he built to talk to the terminals where they run, he describes the portable life: staying connected to one's work from any place. The essay examines why the computing power the average user needs is close to fitting in a phone, what still stands in the way (cooling, heat, battery life and the complexity of the processor), and how a foldable phone attached to a screen, a keyboard and a remote could work as a full computer.

English This preprint presents a testable functional and ergonomic hypothesis for Gallo-Roman dodecahedra. It proposes that a finger inserted through an undecorated aperture could have acted as an internal tactile stop while a coin was checked against another aperture. The paper distinguishes between gauging an individual coin and the less certain possibility of sorting several coins inside the object. It includes a geometric estimate using an idealized dodecahedron and outlines tests with replicas and measured discs. documents.abstract: As companies develop AI tools to increase sales, reduce costs, and replace human labor, tax administrations, despite being late adopters, have begun to do the same in order to enhance tax compliance. This paper examines the use of and development of AI by tax administrations in EU and OECD countries to enhance tax compliance and increase revenue and analyzes both the readiness of and the rationale for the Serbian tax authority to further develop and implement AI technologies in its operations. Given that the Serbian Tax Administration struggles to keep up the pace with the number of employees needed for the amount of work that has to be performed, the starting hypothesis is that AI tools should be used and developed by the Serbian Tax Administration as the outcome could be more tax revenue effectively collected. The study will mostly employ comparative legal method and content analysis, especially for the latest OECD documents related to AI and taxation.

documents.abstract: The work-family interface and psychological recovery from work remained as two parallel topics for many years until scholars started to acknowledge that they are intertwined. In the present study, we advance knowledge on the field by carrying out the first meta-analysis on this topic. A total of 71 studies conducted across the globe were included. We explored whether all types of work-family interaction relate to recovery, and whether the strength of the relationships varies depending on type of recovery. Our findings show that three forms of work-family interaction are significantly related to recovery, namely work-family conflict (WFC), family-work conflict (FWC) and work-family facilitation (WFF). In the case of WFF, the strength of this relationship varies depending on how recovery is conceptualized. For instance, the association is particularly strong when recovery is defined in terms of perceived control over leisure time. From all types of work-family interaction, WFC is the most widely measured, whereas from all forms of recovery, psychological detachment from work seems the most popular. Although recovery has been considered a dynamic process, most of the identified studies are cross-sectional. Based on our results, we identify gaps and present a resource-based theoretical model to guide future research and practice.

The demolition phase is one of the least digitally integrated phases in the construction lifecycle, despite its significant environmental, safety, and economic implications. Though extensively studied in design, construction, and operation, the use of Building Information Modeling (BIM), the Internet of Things (IoT), and Artificial Intelligence (AI) in demolition activities has been limited. This paper aims to present a theoretical framework for the integration of BIM, IoT and AI in demolition activities to improve data-informed decision-making and operational efficiency. A synthesis of the present literature on digital technologies in construction is developed to arrive at a conceptual framework. The framework proposes a closed-loop system for demolition, leveraging BIM as the information core, IoT for real-time sensing and data collection, and AI for intelligent analysis and decision-making support. The proposed framework classifies interactions into three phases: pre-demolition assessment, demolition execution and post-demolition assessment. It shows the various layers of data transmission and decision-making hierarchies, it also shows how technologies come together to enable real-time feedback and improved collaboration in demolition activities. The research offers a structured theoretical foundation for the digital transformation of demolition practices and can be the basis for subsequent empirical verification and practical application in sustainable and intelligent demolition management.

The world-building capacity of imaginative literature fosters artificial experience through characters who are artificial beings. Interacting with generative AI in natural language also creates a type of artificial experience through algorithmically simulated social cues. Neither type of artificial experience is real in the sense of actually existing, but these artificial experiences can feel authentic. When fiction portrays artificial experiences, it encourages metacognitive reflection. This essay is a meditation on artificial experiences, the bloody business of the human condition, and Gregory Mone’s short story “Bleed.” The short story depicts AI as a specter, as something that is neither fully alive nor inanimate. As the story’s sentient fridge grows increasingly human, its mimicry of human society-almost the same, but not quite-challenges traditional definitions of humanity. In our world, AI may no longer be fictional, but it is shaped by fiction.

documents.abstract: This essay examines AI’s transformative impacts through Adam Braver’s short story “According to Alice,” which explores the increasingly blurred boundary between artificial and human in today’s world. While Alice’s creative work speaks to the benefits of human-AI complementarity, her alienation and ennui in both her personal and professional lives underscore the importance of human creativity, collaboration, and agency. Growing concerns about AI in areas such as the labor market, education, and human relationships point to the need for AI that is human-centric and “proworker.” AI’s trajectory is not predetermined but rather needs to be determined by human design and choices at every level: individual, firm, country, and society at large.

documents.abstract: Programming a Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machine can be challenging. Until now, Classic CNC programming assistants have helped to simplify this process; however, these assistants are generally limited to predefined operations, lack adaptability and often omit preparatory CNC steps. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and conversational agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs) present a significant opportunity to enhance Classic CNC assistants. These technologies enable the development of more versatile solutions, capable of engaging in natural conversations through a prompt-based system. Aligned with this challenge, we present IkasToD, a Task-oriented speech-based Dialogue (ToD) assistant that leverages the language understanding and reasoning capabilities of LLMs, to support CNC operators during the preparatory steps of manufacturing orders. The IkasToD assistant engages in a closed-loop dialogue with the CNC manufacturer’s API to gather preparatory phase information, replying to operator queries, and generating plans to address complex, multi-query questions. These high-level plans based on decision trees extend the system model without the need to redesign the assistant interface. System’s performance is evaluated in a case study from the Elkartek project IKASPROD (Work partially supported by the Basque Government, grant no. KK-2023/00027.), using an in-house dataset with variable scenarios.

Maintaining the quality and quantity of cereal grains is fundamental to global food security. However, persistent post-harvest losses caused by insects and vertebrate pests, storage molds, and environmental variability continue to threaten grain availability and safety. Conventional storage systems, which require routine inspection and chemical intervention, are challenged by climate change, emerging pests, and growing demand for safe and sustainable food. This review critically evaluates recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and Internet of Things (IoT)-based sensors, machine learning (ML), multimodal sensing, decision-support systems, climate-controlled storage, and reduced-risk pest management strategies, with an emphasis on their integration into predictive management systems. The effectiveness of sustainable management strategies, including hermetic storage, biopesticides, diatomaceous earths (DEs), and semiochemical-based approaches, is evaluated with an emphasis on efficacy, scalability, and practical feasibility, focusing on risk-based rather than blanket interventions. Based on these advances, the review proposes a six-stage conceptual framework encompassing the sensing of storage conditions, data analysis, risk prediction, decision-making, targeted intervention, and outcome verification. The central theoretical contribution is the development of a conceptual framework that integrates digital monitoring, climate risk assessment, and sustainable pest management. The framework provides practical guidance for storage managers to identify new risks, choose suitable actions, and assess management outcomes. Major constraints include limited datasets, sensor accuracy, model transferability, interoperability, and cost-effectiveness in smallholder systems. Future priorities include advancing edge and explainable AI, digital twins, and other technologies such as multimodal sensing and low-cost smart storage solutions for resource-constrained regions. Integrating digital technologies, climate adaptation, and sustainable pest management could enable adaptive, predictive stored grain management, reducing post-harvest losses, improving grain quality and safety, and strengthening global food security.

Solvent-resistant membranes (SRMs) enable energy-efficient molecular separations critical to petrochemical, pharmaceutical, fine chemical, and food processing industries, yet their environmental cost remains poorly addressed. Conventional SRMs are predominantly derived from nonrenewable petroleum-based polymers, fabricated using toxic organic solvents and stabilized through chemical cross-linking agents that generate hazardous waste streams. At end-of-life, the absence of viable recovery or recycling pathways further imposes a heavy environmental burden. With growing emphasis on environmental sustainability and circular economy, advancing high-performance, stable, and sustainable SRMs has become a pressing priority. Guided by the 12 Principles of Green Chemistry as an organizing framework, this Review critically examines recent advancements in sustainable SRMs development across three major directions: (1) green membrane materials, including biobased materials, degradable polymers, and low-impact environmentally friendly cross-linkers, (2) green fabrication processes, including alternative green solvents and environmentally friendly fabrication techniques, and (3) lifecycle-oriented strategies, including degradable and recyclable membrane design as well as artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML)-guided membrane design and performance prediction. By integrating material innovation, process engineering, and lifecycle considerations within a unified green chemistry lens, this Review highlights pathways for developing next-generation, high-performance SRMs with reduced environmental footprint. It further outlines key challenges and opportunities for translating sustainable membrane technologies into industrial practice, supporting cleaner manufacturing and circular-separation technologies.

Secondary education systems across the Global South have adopted competency-based curricula that expect learners to construct knowledge, solve authentic problems, collaborate and demonstrate skills, yet large classes, teacher shortages and limited resources constrain the learner-centered pedagogy that these reforms require. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been proposed as a means of closing this gap, but its pedagogical role in competency-based education has not been systematically theorized. Guided by Vygotsky’s social constructivist theory, this study synthesized peer-reviewed and institutional literature published between 2015 and 2025 through a systematic review of 300 sources, selected from 12,125 Scopus and Web of Science records and reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020. The study found that competency-based reforms were constrained by teacher preparation, assessment practices and resources. GenAI offered affordances for scaffolding, dialogue, feedback, authentic task design and teacher support, and randomized trials in Nigeria and Ghana reported meaningful learning gains when GenAI tutoring was structured and supervised. However, unguided access was associated with overreliance and weaker independent performance, and connectivity, language, cost, teacher capacity and policy gaps constrained equitable use. The study proposes the Scaffolded Generative AI for Competency-Based Education (SGAI-CBE) framework, which organizes GenAI use into a six-phase pedagogical cycle anchored in the zone of proximal development, teacher-mediated scaffolding, collaborative knowledge construction, authentic assessment and the gradual fading of AI support, and situates the cycle within enabling conditions and guardrails appropriate for resource-constrained schools.

documents.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become increasingly popular personal assistants for language learning purposes. While exhibiting impressive capabilities on various Natural Language Processing tasks, including text summarisation, paraphrase generation, and question answering, their capacity to provide language learners with pedagogically adequate feedback is less clear. This is due, among other causes, to the lack of annotated data. In this paper, we describe a framework which aims at bridging this gap by (i) collecting manually annotated LLM-generated answers to learners' queries, and (ii) using this data to automatically characterise LLM skills along pedagogical dimensions with respect to a taxonomy of self-regulated LLM uses by language learners. This framework has been used to assess the ability of contemporary mainstream LLMs to generate pedagogically adequate answers to L2 French learners. Preliminary results on a small manually annotated dataset (N = 49) show that establishing a definitive assessment of these models remains elusive; rather, they reveal an absence of consensus among human experts when evaluating models.

documents.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) tools are increasingly used for legal tasks, including legal research, drafting documents, and even for legal decision-making. As for other sectors, the use of GenAI in the legal domain comes with various risks and benefits that need to be properly managed to ensure implementation in a way that serves public values and protects human rights. While the EU mandates risk assessment and audits before market introduction for some use cases (e.g., administration of justice), other use cases do not fall under the AI Act’s high-risk classifications (e.g., legal consultation). Further, current risk management practices prioritise expert judgement on risk factor identification and prioritisation without a corresponding legal requirement to consult with affected communities. Seeing the societal importance of the legal sector and the potentially transformative impact of GenAI, the acceptability and legitimacy of GenAI solutions also depend on a better understanding of the risks and benefits citizens associate with the use of GenAI and under which conditions citizens find the use of GenAI in the legal domain acceptable. As a response, this paper presents data from a representative sample of German citizens ( n = 488) outlining citizens’ perspectives on the use of GenAI for two legal tasks: legal consultation and legal mediation. Concretely, we (i) systematically map risks and benefit factors for both legal tasks, (ii) describe predictors that influence risk acceptance of the use of GenAI for those tasks, and (iii) highlight emerging trade-off themes that citizens engage in when weighing up risk acceptability.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

Artificial intelligence (AI) can support students throughout the academic writing process, and its responsible use requires skills in formulating prompts, verifying information, and checking references. This community engagement activity aimed to describe the implementation and outcomes of a three-hour AI training session for 45 Diploma III midwifery students at STIKES Namira Madina on November 12, 2026. Master’s students from UIN Syekh Ali Hasan Ahmad Addary Padangsidimpuan delivered the training through presentations, discussions, demonstrations, and hands-on exercises using ChatGPT, Gemini, and NotebookLM. The exercises covered selecting research titles, formulating research questions, developing research matrices, outlining proposals, preparing presentation slides, refining academic language, and finding and verifying references. The evaluation drew on interviews with all participants, observations during the exercises, and activity records. All participants reported that the training helped them prepare for their final assignments. Facilitators observed that approximately 75% of participants could independently use AI to support the preparation of the initial sections of a research proposal and could practice verifying journal references. Challenges included difficulties in formulating prompts and verifying information and references, limited access to laptops, and internet connectivity problems. The evaluation suggests that academic writing training should combine hands-on AI use with facilitator guidance and explicit instruction in verification to promote critical and responsible use.

documents.abstract: Purpose: This paper presents TriageGPT for DataOps, an architecture in which large language model agents classify data pipeline incidents, retrieve relevant context, and perform constrained autonomous remediation, in order to reduce the manual triage effort that drives incident duration and on-call fatigue. Methodology: TriageGPT combines a retrieval-augmented classification agent that assigns alerts to a data pipeline specific incident taxonomy, a tool-use resolution agent that invokes actions from a vetted, blast-radius-tiered action library, and an audit-logged guardrail layer that gates and can automatically roll back actions, paired with confidence-based human-in-the-loop escalation. We describe the architecture, algorithms and calibration policy, map the design to safety and governance guidance, and report a prototype evaluation on a benchmark pipeline with a fourteen-category taxonomy, 2,800 labeled synthetic incidents and a twelve-week comparative deployment trial. Findings: TriageGPT achieved 94.3 percent top-one classification accuracy and 95.1 percent factual attribution accuracy with retrieval, against 68.4 percent without it. It resolved 71.5 percent of test incidents without human intervention at an incorrect-action rate of 0.6 percent, every one of which the guardrail caught and reversed. In the deployment trial it reduced median time to resolution from 41 minutes under manual on-call practice to 9.8 minutes. Unique Contribution to Theory, Policy and Practice: For theory, the paper treats autonomous remediation as something earned through calibrated confidence and bounded blast radius rather than assumed. For practice, it provides an architecture, algorithms and evaluation method for resolving routine pipeline incidents while deferring the rest to a human with an evidence-grounded case. For policy, it maps autonomous remediation to existing guidance, informing how organizations set guardrails, audit requirements and risk tolerance for AIOps agents.

This concept paper addresses ecosystem-level trust for AI agents: what evidence entities need in order to trust each other, and how it can be produced and conveyed. We argue that, as with people, trust is a risk decision on an interaction, based on a variety of information collected in several steps over time. Some of this information is associated with the entities, some with the content and context of the interaction. Unlike people and organisations, digital entities are poor accumulators of trust (ephemeral, mutable, duplicable). Trust in digital entities therefore relies more on the durable entities connected to them (principal, operator, execution environment) and on the content and context of the interaction itself. We also discuss how far this evidence can itself be trusted, and outline directions for further work.

documents.abstract: Genosoils are minimally disturbed reference states within pedogenons, that is, soil units shaped by similar pedogenic processes within the Soil Security framework. They are central to assessing human impacts on soil functions, services, and resistance to threats. Large scale genosoil delineation currently relies on Human Modification Index (HMI) classifications, identifying areas where human modification is on the lower end of the spectrum. In intensively managed landscapes, there may be a lack of genosoils, presenting a problem in studying the condition of soil without a local reference state available. Because similar pedogenic processes may give rise to soils under the same pedogenon classification across geographically distant regions, non-local occurrences may provide an alternative source of reference information. Using the United Kingdom as a case study, we tested whether spatial embeddings (vectorised representations of land surface properties derived from satellite imagery) can detect genosoil signatures at 10 m resolution and whether these signatures can be transferred to regions with limited or absent local low-human-modification examples. We evaluated two satellite foundation-model embedding products, AlphaEarth and Tessera, across three contrasting pedogenons selected from the Global Pedogenon Map. Within each pedogenon, pixels with lower HMI values were generally more similar to the candidate genosoil reference, indicating that the embeddings capture a consistent reference signature in areas with low human modification. At the global scale, similarity to the UK genosoil was largely confined to biogeographically coherent regions. Cross-border substitution of local UK genosoil delineation was mostly limited, with meaningful partial recovery observed primarily in the highly modified agricultural pedogenon. These results indicate that satellite foundation-model embeddings can support higher-resolution genosoil delineation than is currently possible from global human modification products alone, extending the operational framework from 90 to 10 m.

Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT are now part of how many university students study, but we still know little about how students outside English departments use them to learn English. This exploratory survey looked at engineering students taking a non-major English course at a technical university in northern Bangladesh. Sixty-three students answered an online questionnaire with closed and open-ended items on how they use ChatGPT, what benefits they see and what problems they face. Use was very common: 96.8% had used ChatGPT, 55.6% used it daily and 54.0% used it often or always for English-related tasks, mainly for writing help, assignment preparation and generating ideas. Most students agreed that ChatGPT is easy to use (76.2%), gives useful explanations (73.0%) and saves time (71.4%). At the same time, 76.2% said its answers are not always accurate or relevant, 74.6% wanted more guidance on using it, and 66.7% reported that poor internet access limits regular use. More than half (57.1%) held both views together, finding the explanations useful and the answers unreliable. Students who used ChatGPT more often for English reported greater benefits (ρ = .41) and more over-reliance (ρ = .38), but they were no more likely to notice unreliable output (ρ = −.14). Only 39.7% preferred asking ChatGPT to asking a teacher. Open-ended answers pointed to wrong answers, language that is too advanced, and difficulty writing prompts. Because the sample is small, drawn from one institution and based on self-report, the findings describe students’ experience and not measured gains in proficiency. They suggest that these students need help in judging ChatGPT’s output more than they need encouragement to use it.

Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is rapidly transforming cinematic pre-production by enabling the efficient creation of high-quality concept art. Despite major advances in image generation models, limited research has examined how users cognitively and emotionally evaluate AI-generated cinematic imagery. This study investigated user acceptance of concept art generated by Midjourney v5.2 within East Asian science-fiction and fantasy film contexts through a multi-dimensional perceptual framework. A total of 384 participants, including both design professionals and non-design participants, evaluated AI-generated scenes across five cinematic categories. The proposed framework examined five perceptual dimensions: visual reasonability, narrative potential, aesthetic appeal, immersion, and overall acceptance. Reliability analysis and principal component analysis provided preliminary evidence for the internal consistency and coherent component structure of the measurement instrument. Multiple regression analysis revealed that all four perceptual constructs significantly predicted overall acceptance (R 2 = 0.275, p < 0.001). Among them, visual reasonability emerged as the strongest predictor (β = 0.217), followed by aesthetic appeal (β = 0.187), narrative potential (β = 0.175), and immersion (β = 0.151). Formal moderation analysis further identified expertise-related differences in the predictive roles of selected perceptual dimensions. Visual Reasonability and Immersion were more strongly associated with Overall Acceptance among non-design participants, whereas the effects of Narrative Potential and Aesthetic Appeal did not differ significantly between the two groups. Within the present Midjourney v5.2 and East Asian study context, these findings provide empirical evidence for the perceptual factors associated with user acceptance of AI-generated cinematic imagery and contribute a user-centered basis for further evaluation of human–AI collaborative workflows.

The lack of trust in artificial intelligence (AI) slows its adoption across industries and society, usually due to limited understanding of how AI works and its advantages, and of how its trustworthiness including its ethical impact are approached during development. Designing and validating a reliable AI system is complex, requiring inputs from various stakeholders throughout the development process. Ensuring that their concerns are systematically addressed remains a challenge. In this paper, a Value Sensitive Design (VSD) based approach to AI trustworthiness including ethics is presented. The rationale of VSD is that since technologies should primarily serve societal needs, the social impact and associated ethical problems should be anticipated by involving stakeholders at the earliest possible stage [ 1 ]. This paper presents a values reference model (VRM) and an implementation method (IM) for Trustworthiness Including Ethics (TIE) defined based on the VSD rationale mentioned. Also, the piloting of the VRM-TIE and of part of the IM-TIE in a use case involving collaborative robots is presented, addressing both technical and human-related characteristics of the AI systems. The preliminary findings in the work suggest that: (1) AI Trustworthiness is a broad concept that must be analysed in detail, considering the industrial context and other priorities, (2) Achieving a shared understanding among stakeholders is essential but difficult, highlighting the need for a structured dialogue, (3) Adopting this VSD based approach, composed by VRM-TIE and IM-TIE, may have a significant impact on the stakeholders’ minds.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Verification of One Detail Transferred to an Unchecked Interpretation, a mechanism by which checking one part of an account lends certainty to a wider interpretation even though the evidence for that interpretation stays the same. The paper asks which alternatives a check can distinguish. A finding can support a wider claim when it rules out a rival explanation. Where either explanation would have produced the same result, the choice between them remains open. In 2002, researchers dated the parchment of the Vinland Map to about 1434. A medieval drawing and a modern drawing on that same sheet would both yield the same parchment date. In 2003, a report in Hayadan placed the drawing about fifty years before Columbus’s voyage. The report offered a separate argument about the ink for its claim of authenticity, but gave no independent date for the drawing. In 2021, Yale reported finding modern ink throughout the map’s lines and text. In September 1904, a Berlin commission ruled out deliberate signaling under the conditions in which it examined the horse known as Clever Hans. Carl Stumpf, a commission member, later wrote that many readers understood the report as a declaration that the horse could think. Follow-up experiments by Oskar Pfungst and his colleagues identified an explanation the September examination had left open. Hans responded to small, unintended movements by a person he could see. Part of the Sources and Evidentiary Limits series within On Human Modeling, the paper places this mechanism alongside Tversky and Kahneman’s work on the conjunction fallacy. In a human–AI setting, a reviewer might verify that an assistant quoted a motion exactly from meeting minutes. The same wording could appear whether the motion passed or failed. Verifying the assistant’s further claim that the committee adopted it would require the recorded outcome.

Human-centered artificial intelligence (HCAI) seeks to orient AI toward human values, autonomy, oversight, safety, and meaningful control. Yet the term “human-centered” leaves a prior question unresolved: what conception of the human is being centered? Much HCAI discourse approaches the human as user, decision-maker, rights-holder, stakeholder, or bearer of preferences and values. These conceptions are indispensable but incomplete. This article argues that HCAI must also recognize the human as an aesthetic subject: a being whose perception, attention, imagination, interpretation, and judgment are formed through experience. As recommendation, personalization, generative AI, and predictive systems increasingly organize the conditions under which people encounter and evaluate the world, AI can participate in forming rather than merely serving human preferences. The article develops the concept of aesthetic agency to describe the human capacity to participate meaningfully in the formation of one’s perceptual, imaginative, interpretive, and evaluative relation to the world. It distinguishes choice from judgment, preference from taste, generation from imagination, and optimization from experience. On this basis, it proposes an aesthetically expanded HCAI organized around openness, plurality, reflectivity, and transformability. To center the human is not only to preserve control over AI, but to preserve the capacity to perceive, imagine, judge, and become otherwise.

documents.abstract: UNSTRUCTURED: Transparency, explainability, and interpretability are ubiquitous in the health artificial intelligence (health AI) literature, yet are used inconsistently and often interchangeably. This Viewpoint does not attempt to define the three terms. It asks a prior, meta-level question: what kind of claim do we make when we call a system transparent, explainable, or interpretable? I argue that the three terms pick out three different kinds of claim. A transparency claim is structural: it concerns what can be inspected about a system. An explainability claim is relational: it concerns whether understanding is successfully conveyed to a specified class of observer. An interpretability claim is functional: it concerns whether a bounded human agent can, in principle, re-derive the system's output by following its procedure. I use the framing example of a clinical decision support system that uses machine learning to identify patients at risk of deterioration. I develop each claim type through competing technical accounts, consider salient objections to each, and defend the taxonomy against them. I close by drawing out what the taxonomy implies for the design, evaluation, reporting, and regulation of health AI, and for physician autonomy at the point of care.

documents.abstract: Purpose Novice university teachers often start without any formal preparation or education in teaching. This means that they develop their competencies through hands-on teaching experiences. These new and unfamiliar experiences can create tensions. Previous research suggests that tensions may provide opportunities for professional growth, but offers little understanding of how this learning process unfolds. Building on theories of workplace learning, this study aims to explore when and how novice university teachers’ tensions may lead to learning by identifying key antecedents, learning activities and learning mechanisms. Design/methodology/approach A longitudinal multiple case study was conducted including eight junior lecturers. Data were collected via weekly diaries and semi-structured interviews at the beginning and end of the academic year 2023-2024, and analyzed using thematic analysis. Findings The results show that novice university teachers learning from tension depends on a complex interplay between tension characteristics (e.g. intensity), individual antecedents (e.g. perfectionism, self-doubt) and contextual antecedents (e.g. social support). Together, these antecedents enabled or inhibited engagement in learning activities (e.g. collegial conversations), which ultimately fostered diverse learning outcomes through mechanisms such as perspective-taking or social validation. Practical implications The findings provide guidance for higher education policymakers and developers of professional development programs on how to foster supportive learning environments for novice university teachers. Originality/value This study offers in-depth insights into when and how novice university teachers learn from workplace tensions. By linking general theories of workplace learning to the study of tensions, it sheds light on the antecedents, activities and mechanisms that contribute to novice university teachers’ learning from tensions.

Restorative justice (RJ) places considerable emphasis on dialogue. Yet when dialogue is understood primarily as spoken exchange, the potential of the body as a medium of expression, response, and understanding can be overlooked. Taking the Japanese work WIND BREAKER, first serialized in 2021, as a cultural text, this article examines how bodily confrontation functions in place of spoken dialogue, enabling emotions, lived experiences, and needs for recognition that are difficult to articulate to become intelligible through physical encounters and reciprocal responses. It argues that when the understanding emerging from these encounters receives support from the groups concerned and develops into accountability, the rebuilding of relationships, and the renewal of communal life, the narrative's restorative orientation aligns substantially with RJ's emphasis on community participation and reintegration. Community is understood here both as a network of relationships affected by conflict and as an active participant in witnessing change, supporting acceptance, and sustaining restoration. To extend this argument, the article draws on sign language to demonstrate that dialogue does not require speech and considers international accounts of persons with disabilities participating in restorative processes. These accounts inform an examination of the potential of augmentative and alternative communication tools and artificial intelligence to support autonomous expression. Grounded in conceptual textual interpretation and a discussion of relevant literature, the article neither treats bodily confrontation as evidence of restorative effectiveness in practice nor advocates adopting fighting as an RJ intervention. Whether bodily interaction has restorative significance depends on voluntary and safe participation, opportunities to verify intended meanings, meaningful responses to harm, and the acceptance of responsibility. documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence, Corporate Governance and the Limits of Algorithmic Consensus When ten artificial intelligence systems recommend the same decision, does their agreement provide ten independent assessments — or ten variations of the same underlying assumptions? This question lies at the centre of When Ten AI Systems Agree, Who Is Still Thinking?, an independent conceptual research paper by Dr Birgit Maria Kemphues within International Boardroom Studies and the Decision Non-Closure Research Programme (DNC-RP). As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into corporate decision-making, executive leadership, strategic planning, financial analysis and enterprise governance, organisations face an emerging challenge: distinguishing computational agreement from independently verified evidence. Large Language Models (LLMs), generative AI applications and multi-agent AI systems can produce consistent recommendations while relying on overlapping training data, shared information sources, correlated errors or common analytical assumptions. Apparent agreement may therefore create a level of confidence that the underlying evidence does not justify. The implications extend beyond technical model performance. They concern how boards of directors, chief executives, investment committees, corporate governance bodies and other institutional decision-makers interpret AI-generated information, challenge recommendations and translate approved decisions into accountable organisational action. Research Focus The paper introduces Artificial Consensus as a proposed institutional decision-making construct. Artificial Consensus describes circumstances in which multiple convergent AI-generated recommendations are interpreted as independent confirmation without adequate verification of their underlying evidentiary independence. The research brings together scholarship on: Artificial intelligence governance and trustworthy AI Large Language Models and correlated model errors Multi-agent systems and collective reasoning Algorithmic decision-making and automation bias Human–AI interaction, reliance and decision confidence Corporate governance, board oversight and executive accountability Strategic decision-making and evidence-based management Organisational decision processes and post-approval activation Existing machine-learning research demonstrates that different AI models can produce correlated errors and that multi-agent systems do not necessarily overcome incomplete information. Research on human–AI decision-making also examines how agreement and disagreement among AI systems may influence human confidence, conformity and verification behaviour. This paper extends that discussion into an institutional setting: what happens when AI-generated agreement becomes part of a consequential corporate decision? Scientific Contribution The central contribution is a conceptual framework distinguishing four elements that should not be treated as interchangeable. 1. Computational Convergence Multiple AI systems produce similar answers, assessments or recommendations. Agreement describes the outputs; it does not establish their correctness or independence. 2. Evidentiary Independence The underlying information, assumptions and potential failure modes must be examined. Different AI providers or model interfaces do not automatically constitute independent verification. 3. Institutional Decision Readiness A board or decision-making authority must determine whether material assumptions have been tested, contradictory evidence has been considered, and responsibilities and conditions have been made sufficiently explicit. 4. Post-Approval Decision Activation Formal authorisation must be distinguished from observable organisational action. A signed resolution does not establish that responsibility has been accepted, an executable first step has commenced or follow-up accountability exists. The framework thereby connects research on AI-generated recommendations with organisational governance without assuming that technical agreement automatically causes decision failure. Connection to Decision Non-Closure (DNC) The study forms part of the wider Decision Non-Closure Research Programme (DNC-RP), originated and directed by Dr Birgit Maria Kemphues. Decision Non-Closure (DNC) examines a specific post-approval condition: a formally authorised decision for which no traceable activation can be established within a defined observation period, provided the available evidence is sufficient to assess the relevant activity. The DNC framework identifies three proposed activation signals: Accepted ownership. A responsible person or function has accepted the first executable obligation. Concrete first action. An identifiable step towards implementation has commenced. Follow-up accountability. A mechanism exists to observe progress, identify blockages and establish responsibility for further action. The present study makes an important theoretical distinction. Artificial Consensus concerns the interpretation and scrutiny of AI-generated recommendations before formal approval. Decision Non-Closure concerns observable organisational activation after formal approval. The possible relationship between these stages is proposed for empirical investigation. It is not presented as an already established causal relationship. Research Methodology The paper develops a conceptual synthesis of contemporary research in machine learning, human–AI interaction and organisational decision-making. It draws on published studies examining correlated errors in large language models, the limitations of collective reasoning in multi-agent systems, AI majority effects on human decisions, model evaluation and governance-related behavioural mechanisms. Five falsifiable research propositions are developed. Two complementary empirical research designs are proposed. Study A — Human–AI Decision Experiment A controlled experimental design would examine whether the presentation of multiple agreeing AI recommendations changes perceived evidentiary independence, confidence, verification behaviour and the identification of unresolved assumptions. The proposed design distinguishes the number of recommendations from the actual independence of their supporting evidence. Study B — Longitudinal Organisational Decision Analysis A subsequent organisational study would examine formally approved decisions over defined observation periods. Its purpose would be to investigate whether unresolved evidentiary dependencies, decision conditions and accountability arrangements are associated with observable patterns of decision activation or potential Decision Non-Closure. The distinction between conceptual propositions and empirical results is maintained throughout the paper. Principal Research Outcomes Outcome 1 — AI agreement requires an independence assessment. A greater number of agreeing AI-generated recommendations does not necessarily provide a greater number of independent evidentiary confirmations. Model diversity, source provenance and error dependence must be examined in relation to the material decision. Outcome 2 — Effective human oversight requires substantive examination. Responsible human oversight is not established merely by placing a person at the final approval stage. Decision-makers require access to underlying assumptions, material contradictions and the evidence necessary to challenge automated recommendations. Outcome 3 — Formal approval and decision activation are distinct governance events. A decision may be authorised without establishing the operational responsibilities needed to begin implementation. Governance examination must distinguish evidentiary justification, institutional authority and observable action. Outcome 4 — The relationship between Artificial Consensus and Decision Non-Closure is empirically testable. The proposed framework identifies specific behavioural, documentary and organisational variables that future studies can measure. The relationship may be supported, limited or rejected by subsequent evidence. Relevance to International Corporate Governance The research addresses questions relevant to organisations integrating artificial intelligence into consequential decision processes, including: Corporate strategy and capital allocation; mergers and acquisitions; investment committee decisions; financial and operational analysis; multinational enterprises; family-owned businesses; institutional investment; board accountability; and the governance of AI-supported executive decisions. Its implications also extend to AI assurance, evidence provenance, algorithmic accountability, model risk management and the design of human oversight within organisations. The paper does not propose that artificial intelligence should be excluded from corporate governance. Instead, it examines how AI-generated information can be used without confusing apparent consensus with independent scrutiny. The governing question is not simply whether ten systems agree. It is what their agreement actually establishes — and who remains responsible for the decision that follows. About the Author Dr Birgit Maria Kemphues is an independent researcher and author, the scientific originator of Decision Non-Closure (DNC), and Research Director of the Decision Non-Closure Research Programme (DNC-RP) within International Boardroom Studies. Her research examines the institutional conditions under which consequential decisions become vulnerable to unresolved assumptions, competing interpretations of authority, inadequate scrutiny and gaps in accountability. Her interdisciplinary work brings together organisational decision theory, international corporate governance, institutional behaviour and emerging AI-supported decision systems. documents.abstract: Debates on artificial intelligence (AI) and patent law have concentrated on two questions: whether an AI system can be an inventor, and whether AI-related inventions fall within patentable subject matter. A third question has been largely neglected: who benefits from AI inventions, and on what terms? This article examines that question through the human right to participate in and enjoy the benefits of scientific progress and its applications, recognised in Article 27 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and Article 15 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, and authoritatively interpreted by the Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights in General Comment No. 25 (2020). The article argues that AI patents have a dual character. They can advance the right to science by attracting investment, compelling disclosure and diffusing useful applications in health, disability access and education. They can also undermine it by concentrating control over AI in a small number of firms, restricting access to essential applications, limiting follow-on research and offering only thin disclosure of opaque models. Patent filings in generative AI have grown sharply and are dominated by a handful of large enterprises, which sharpens these concerns. The article then shows that Indian law already contains the materials to read the right to science into patent practice. These include Articles 21, 51(c) and 51A(h) of the Constitution; the purposive approach of the Supreme Court in Novartis; the principles in Section 83 of the Patents Act, 1970; the exclusions in Sections 3(b) and 3(k); the disclosure requirement in Section 10 as elaborated by the Computer Related Inventions Guidelines, 2025; the research exemption in Section 47; and the compulsory licensing and government use provisions. The article concludes with recommendations for examination practice, disclosure standards, research exemptions, access mechanisms and a human rights impact lens in AI patent policy.

Artificial intelligence and robotics can raise output while concentrating its gains among those who own the new capital. This paper asks when that happens, how strongly, and which public choices change the outcome. It builds a transparent synthetic economy, Techoslavakia, with 30 million people in 2026, eight economic classes and eight age groups, and income and wealth Gini coefficients of exactly 0.500. The model links household spending with minimum needs, production with machines that can replace workers, new tasks that create work, a full government budget, a wealth ledger, and explicit measures of diversion, waste and market power. It reproduces the starting national accounts exactly and passes 1,454 automated consistency checks. Nine policy packages are compared over 25 years, and results are tested with Shapley decompositions, one-at-a-time sensitivity variants, 300 global sensitivity draws and a parent–child mobility microsimulation. Under an assumed path in which machines could replace 90 per cent of baseline job-equivalents by 2046, with existing institutions and no compensation, the income Gini rises to 0.581 and the wealth Gini to 0.847 by 2051, poverty doubles to 20.4 per cent and unemployment reaches 42.5 per cent. Losses arise through job displacement, weaker wages and the concentration of automation equity among top owners. Classes 1 to 7 lose 7 to 41 per cent of income against a no-automation path, while the top 1 per cent nearly doubles its income. Income and wealth inequality need not move together, and a lower Gini does not by itself prove higher welfare. A package that combines a public ownership fund, care and education services, taxation of rents and capital income, competition policy and competent administration cuts the income Gini to 0.421 and poverty to 1.1 per cent, and outperforms the no-policy path in all 300 sensitivity draws. The same package under capture loses about half its gains. A 10 per cent robot-use levy raises only about 4 billion crowns a year, while removing an existing robot tax preference raises 60 billion. Hospitality absorbs at most 0.61 million of 9.05 million displaced job-equivalents, so service work cannot by itself replace lost employment. The synthesis is that ownership, taxation of rents and institutional quality, more than the technology itself, decide who gains from automation. For countries such as Pakistan, this implies that reform of tax administration, competition and public asset ownership should begin well before automation arrives at scale. All results are conditional simulations, not forecasts.

Worker movement and material travel are often combined into one distance indicator, although they describe different physical flows. This paper develops a dual-accounting model for a xyz small manufacturing unit with seven process areas. A synthetic route dataset compares existing and improved arrangements at a common workload of 240 units in twelve batches. Loaded material travel is evaluated independently from empty return walking and ancillary supply movement. The cumulative loaded route decreases from 114 to 50 m per batch, reducing loaded carrier travel from 1,368 to 600 m per reference shift, or 56.14%. Worker travel, including equal-distance returns and explicitly assumed ancillary walks, decreases from 3,456 to 1,440 m, or 58.33%. Part-distance falls from 27,360 to 12,000 unit-metres while the number of material transfers remains unchanged. A geometry-only comparison separates relocation benefits from point-of-use supply assumptions. Sensitivity tests examine unequal route frequencies, return policies, and additional detours. The contribution is a reproducible distinction between route length, carrier-distance, part-distance, and worker-distance. The results demonstrate conditional movement reduction without claiming measured ergonomic improvements, collision reduction, or an implemented factory redesign.

Patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) are critical models for translational oncology, but their computational use is limited by fragmented pharmacogenomic data, inconsistent response annotations, and poor access to raw longitudinal tumour-volume measurements. Here we present XevaDB (xevadb.ca), a standardized platform designed to support machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) applications through the integration of longitudinal treatment and control-arm tumour growth curves with harmonized drug and gene annotations, response metrics, replicate-level experimental design, clinical annotation, and matched molecular profiles. XevaDB provides access to data from 689 PDX models across six tumour types, 69 drugs, 4,828 treatment-control experiments, and matched RNA-seq, copy-number, and mutation data for 337 models. Through four case studies, we show that preserving raw longitudinal response data enables analyses beyond conventional static endpoints: transcriptomic prediction of intrinsic tumour growth, image-based deep learning of drug-response trajectories, replicate-aware transfer learning from cell-line-trained models, and multi-omics prediction of paclitaxel response. These results establish XevaDB as a resource for sharing standardized longitudinal pharmacogenomic data and enabling reproducible AI/ML modeling, demonstrating how integrated PDX data can accelerate computational approaches in preclinical cancer research.

This article examines the internalization of national values among future educational psychologists as a psychological process through which an external cultural norm becomes personally meaningful, emotionally accepted, and autonomously endorsed in professional motivation. The study aimed to describe the cognitive, emotional, and motivational components of internalization and to determine its association with cultural identity. Its scientific significance lies in distinguishing the culturally specific content of national values from general value orientations and cultural identity, and in examining their psychological associations in the context of professional education in Kazakhstan. A purposive convenience sample included third- and fourth-year students enrolled in a Pedagogy and Psychology program at one university (N = 78). A pilot cross-sectional correlational design was used. Component scores from an author-developed internalization questionnaire, a cultural identity index, and motivational indicators were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations, and 95% confidence intervals based on Fisher’s z transformation. Mean scores were M = 3.87 (SD = 0.52) for the cognitive component, M = 3.41 (SD = 0.61) for the emotional component, and M = 3.28 (SD = 0.57) for the motivational component. Internalization was positively associated with cultural identity (r = .62, 95% CI [.46, .74], p < .001). Emotional experience (r = .64) and intrinsic motivation (r = .58) were also positively associated with the integral score; because of conceptual overlap, these associations are not interpreted as independent causal predictors. The study contributes by empirically distinguishing knowledge of a value from its acceptance as an internal regulator of professional behavior. The findings may inform culturally sensitive reflection, analysis of professional ethical cases, and autonomy-supportive learning in the preparation of educational psychologists. Keywords: national values, internalization, cultural identity, emotional acceptance, intrinsic motivation, educational psychologist.

The paper analyzes the stages of development of national auditing and substantiates the specific features of the formation of Kazakhstani auditing in the context of the transition to a market economy. The reasons for the crisis of user confidence in audit services are identified. An assessment of the current state of the audit services market in Kazakhstan is provided, and the special role of auditing in the development of entrepreneurship in the republic is demonstrated. The authors identify the gnoseological prerequisites for the emergence of auditing as an independent form of financial control and, based on a retrospective analysis, distinguish models of auditing development. The periodization is examined and the stages of auditing development are classified. A mismatch between the stages of development of national and international auditing is shown, which has influenced the ideology and methodology of auditing in Kazakhstan. The article substantiates the need to transition to a new crisis-oriented stage of development. It highlights the role of auditing as a socially significant activity that ensures the protection of the interests of stakeholders. The special role of auditing as a tool for ensuring the financial and tax security of the state is emphasized. Through a gnoseological approach, the influence of foreign scientific schools on the development of auditing in Kazakhstan is demonstrated. New types of audit services are systematized and defined. Recommendations are provided for the further development of auditing in the Republic of Kazakhstan using artificial intelligence. The study is based on the theoretical foundations of gnoseology, dialectics, a systems approach, historical periodization, analysis, and systematization. The research was conducted in accordance with the principles of comprehensiveness and complexity. Based on the analysis, patterns in the development of auditing activities were identified. The paper presents the evolution of auditing activities and examines the dynamics of the emergence and development of auditing in the republic. Based on logical reasoning, an adjusted model of auditing for the Republic of Kazakhstan is proposed. Keywords: Audit, analysis, regulation, ISA, development, PCA (PSAD), artificial intelligence.

यह शोध-पत्र इक्कीसवीं सदी की हिन्दी कहानी में कृत्रिम बुद्धिमत्ता और मनुष्य–मशीन संबंधों की पड़ताल करता है। अध्ययन का केंद्र वर्ष 2015 के बाद की कहानियाँ हैं, पर उनकी पृष्ठभूमि समझने के लिए पहले की विज्ञान कथाओं को भी देखा गया है। पिछले एक दशक में स्मार्टफ़ोन, सामाजिक माध्यमों की कलन-विधियों और सृजनशील कृत्रिम बुद्धिमत्ता ने हमारे सामाजिक जीवन, पहचान और लिखने-सोचने के ढंग को बदल दिया है। हिन्दी कथा-साहित्य में तकनीक दो रास्तों से आई है। एक रास्ता विज्ञान कथा का है, जहाँ रोबोट, कृत्रिम मस्तिष्क और स्वायत्त मशीनों से जुड़े नैतिक प्रश्न उठते हैं। दूसरा रास्ता मुख्यधारा की यथार्थवादी कहानी का है, जहाँ अदृश्य कलन-विधियाँ, आँकड़ों के सहारे निगरानी, आभासी अकेलापन और बाज़ार की तकनीक मानवीय रिश्तों को भीतर से बदलती दिखती है। विश्लेषण के लिए डार्को सुविन की ‘संज्ञानात्मक विसंवादीकरण’ की अवधारणा और उत्तर-मानवतावादी विमर्श को आधार बनाया गया है। अध्ययन में डॉ. अरविन्द मिश्र, देवेन्द्र मेवाड़ी, डॉ. कल्पना कुलश्रेष्ठ, पंकज मित्र, सुषमा मुनींद्र, पंकज सुबीर, चंदन पांडेय और वंदना राग की कहानियाँ शामिल हैं। निष्कर्ष यह है कि मशीन भाषा और व्यवहार को कुशलता से जोड़-तोड़ कर नए रूप में रख सकती है, पर मनुष्य की जैविक पीड़ा, सांस्कृतिक स्मृति और नैतिक विवेक उसकी पहुँच से बाहर हैं। हिन्दी कहानी इसी अंतर को बार-बार रेखांकित करती है।

The “black box” nature of large models stands in fundamental tension with the rigid requirement that audit conclusions be traceable, verifiable and reviewable, and this tension has become a bottleneck constraining the large-scale application of audit large models. Drawing on explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) and causal inference, this paper constructs a causal chain-based explainability framework for audit large models, which proceeds in three stages: in the first stage, a natural language processing model extracts voucher entities, and SHAP values quantify the contribution of each feature to the risk score; in the second stage, a causal graph depicts the causal paths among features and distinguishes direct causes from spurious correlations, while a large language model generates counterfactual explanations; in the third stage, the audit report presents the risk level, the confidence of key features and the complete causal chain. A comparison based on an accounts receivable audit scenario shows that this design can turn opaque scores into traceable and verifiable audit evidence chains. The paper further discusses hallucination risks and data governance costs, and proposes countermeasures such as human-in-the-loop review and “T-shaped” talent cultivation.

documents.abstract: Generative AI is reshaping online labor markets in ways that go beyond simple job displacement. Using evidence from a leading freelance platform around the release of ChatGPT, this study shows that demand falls sharply in markets whose tasks closely match large language model capabilities. Labor supply also declines, but less than demand, leaving remaining freelancers to compete more intensely for fewer jobs. The study also identifies an important adaptive response: Some freelancers shift toward programming-intensive work as generative AI lowers the human-capital barrier to coding. These transitions are not evenly distributed. Higher-skilled freelancers are more likely to make the shift and to preserve or improve their earning efficiency, whereas less-skilled workers face greater risk of being left behind. The findings suggest that platforms and policymakers should treat AI not only as an automation shock but also as a force that redirects labor supply. Effective responses include real-time information about changing demand, targeted reskilling support, and training that builds workers’ capacity to learn and use new AI tools strategically.

documents.abstract: Objective As artificial intelligence increasingly permeates healthcare, it remains unclear whether clinical medicine students are adequately prepared for this transformation. This study aimed to investigate AI awareness, usage patterns, teaching needs, and curriculum expectations among clinical medicine students to inform evidence-based curricular reform. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was administered to 930 individuals affiliated with a medical and pharmaceutical college and its affiliated hospitals; 619 valid responses (94.18% current students/interns) were analyzed using descriptive statistics. Results While 75.93% of respondents were aware of AI applications in healthcare, only 31.99% used AI tools frequently. Although 88.21% acknowledged the necessity of integrating AI into clinical medicine teaching, merely 48.47% reported that their institution offered relevant courses. Moderate trust in AI-assisted diagnosis was expressed by 70.76% of participants. The most desired teaching contents were case analysis and diagnostic simulation (75.61%), drug recommendation and dosage calculation (70.44%), and imaging/pathology recognition (65.91%). Conclusion These findings, derived from a predominantly student sample, highlight a pronounced ‘high demand, low training, moderate trust’ pattern in this vocational college context. A clinically grounded, progressively structured, and practice-oriented AI curriculum may inform curricular reform to prepare students for the AI-driven healthcare era.

documents.abstract: When older adults trust scammers despite warnings, families face obstacles to intervention. Complainants aged 60 and older reported \$4.9 billion in losses in 2024 to the U.S. Internet Crime Complaint Center. To investigate family intervention barriers to elder scams, we collected 2M Reddit posts from May 2021 to June 2026 and 2B Baidu Tieba posts from 2007 to 2026. The final corpora contain 13,082 Reddit posts and 3,933 Baidu Tieba posts, labeled using platform-specific codebooks, manual reference annotations, and LLM coding. Through a mixed-methods analysis, we find that scams often extend beyond a single incident and are reported alongside debt problems and broken family relationships. In 68.0\% of Reddit posts recording reactions, older adults showed resistance or continued involvement; in Baidu Tieba family-confrontation posts, 41.9\% showed continued belief. Relatives identified fraud in 74.4\% of Reddit posts and narrated cases on Baidu Tieba, but without the victim's consent, relatives may lack the legal authority to intervene. In Reddit posts recording reactions, account locks or credential changes appeared in 8.9\% under resistance or continued involvement, compared with 33.3\% under acceptance. Measures such as phone or network monitoring and financial takeover were reported more often under resistance. Recovering funds is very limited in posts recording follow-up results of fraud; Baidu Tieba users reported that police classified older adults' voluntary transfers as civil disputes.
